Towards higher Frobenius functors for symmetric tensor categories
Download PDF
  • Kevin Coulembier1 &
  • Johannes Flake2 

  • 194 Accesses

  • Explore all metrics

Abstract

We develop theory and examples of monoidal functors on tensor categories in positive characteristic that generalise the Frobenius functor from [5, 17, 22]. The latter has proved to be a powerful tool in the ongoing classification of tensor categories of moderate growth, and we demonstrate the similar potential of the generalisations. More explicitly, we describe a new construction of the generalised Verlinde categories \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) in terms of representation categories of elementary abelian p-groups. This leads to families of functors relating to \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) that we conjecture, and partially show, to exhibit the characteristic properties of the Frobenius functor relating to \(\operatorname {Ver}_p\). In particular, we conjecture some of these functors to detect categories that fibre over \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\).

1 Introduction

The structural study of (symmetric) tensor categories over a field, in the sense of [14, 16], typically splits into categories of ‘moderate growth’ and those of ‘superexponential growth’, see [9, 19] and references therein for recent progress in both directions. In the current paper we focus on the former type. In characteristic zero, by classical results of Deligne in [12, 13], all such categories are super-tannakian, meaning they are representation categories of affine group superschemes. By the principle of tannakian reconstruction [12] this is equivalent to saying that all tensor categories of moderate growth admit a tensor functor to (‘fibre over’) the tensor category of supervector spaces \(\textrm{sVec}\).

For the rest of the introduction, we fix a prime p, and work over an algebraically closed field \(\Bbbk \) of characteristic p. Then the situation is much more complicated, and we refer to [1, 2, 5, 6, 9, 10, 15, 17, 22] and references therein for recent progress. We list the results that feature most prominently in the motivation for the current work. The symmetric fusion category \(\operatorname {Ver}_p\), see [22], which can be defined as the semisimplification of the representation category \(\operatorname {Rep}C_p\) of the cyclic group of order p, is an example of a tensor category of moderate growth that is not super-tannakian (when \(p>3\)). In [9], generalising specific cases in [17, 22], it was proved that a tensor category of moderate growth fibres over \(\operatorname {Ver}_p\) if and only if it is ‘Frobenius exact’. The latter condition has many equivalent definitions, see [5, 8, 17]. The definition responsible for the terminology is that a tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\) is Frobenius exact when the Frobenius functor

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {Fr}:\;\mathcal {C}\;\rightarrow \;\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_p\end{aligned}$$
(1.1)

is exact. This symmetric monoidal functor \(\operatorname {Fr}\) is obtained from the p-th power functor \(X\mapsto X^{\otimes p}\) on \(\mathcal {C}\), where we can interpret \(X^{\otimes p}\) as a representation of \(S_p\) or \(C_p<S_p\), combined with the defining semisimplification functor \(\operatorname {Rep}C_p\rightarrow \operatorname {Ver}_p\).

On the other hand, in [1, 2, 6] a chain of (incompressible) tensor categories

$$\begin{aligned} \textrm{Vec}\;\subset \;\textrm{sVec}\;\subset \operatorname {Ver}_p\;\subset \;\operatorname {Ver}_{p^2}\;\subset \; \operatorname {Ver}_{p^3}\;\subset \;\cdots \end{aligned}$$

is constructed where \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) is not Frobenius exact for \(n>1\). In [2, Conjecture 1.4] it is conjectured that any tensor category of moderate growth fibres over \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^\infty }=\cup _n\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\). By [10], this conjecture is equivalent to the conjecture that the only incompressible tensor categories of moderate growth are the tensor subcategories of \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^\infty }\).

1.1 General theory of \(\textbf{O}\)-functors

The aim of this paper, only partially fulfilled thus far, is to construct ‘higher analogues’

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {C}\;\rightarrow \; \mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n} \end{aligned}$$
(1.2)

of \(\operatorname {Fr}\) based on the functor \(X\mapsto X^{\otimes p^n}\), for general \(n\ge 1\). We axiomatise the essential properties of the Frobenius functor (1.1) yielding the notion of \(\textbf{O}_n\)-functors. In general terms, an \(\textbf{O}_n\)-functor is a family of symmetric monoidal functors \(\Phi _\mathcal {C}\) as in Equation (1.2), for each tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\) over \(\Bbbk \), which intertwines tensor functors. We say that an \(\textbf{O}_n\)-functor detects fibering over \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) if, for any tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\) of moderate growth, \(\mathcal {C}\) fibres over \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) if and only if \(\Phi _\mathcal {C}\) is exact. The main theorem of [9] can then be rephrased as stating that \(\operatorname {Fr}\) detects fibering over \(\operatorname {Ver}_p\). Higher versions of the Frobenius functors should be \(\textbf{O}_n\)-functors that detect fibering over \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\).

Using a distinguished generating object V of the categories \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\), a parity involution \(X\mapsto \overline{X}\) on them, and a canonical semisimplification functor to \(\operatorname {Ver}_p\), which allows us to associate to any \(\textbf{O}_n\)-functor \(\Phi \) an \(\textbf{O}_1\)-functor \(\overline{\Phi }\), we show in Theorem 4.3.3:

Theorem A

An \(\textbf{O}_n\)-functor \(\Phi =(\Phi _\mathcal {C})_\mathcal {C}\) detects fibering over \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) if

  • \(\Phi _{\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}}(V)\simeq \overline{\textbf{1}}\boxtimes \overline{V}\) and

  • the \(\textbf{O}_1\)-functor \(\overline{\Phi }\) detects fibering over \(\operatorname {Ver}_p\).

We also show that, without any additional assumptions, any \(\textbf{O}_n\)-functor ‘defines’ some incompressible tensor category, in a way such that the \(\textbf{O}_1\)-functor \(\operatorname {Fr}\) defines \(\operatorname {Ver}_p\). This gives further motivation for the construction of \(\textbf{O}_n\)-functors, although we also show that different \(\textbf{O}_n\)-functors can define the same incompressible category.

1.2 Construction of \(\textbf{O}\)-functors

To obtain concrete instances of potential higher Frobenius functors, we establish a new connection between the representation theory of \(SL_2\) and that of the elementary abelian p-groups \(C_p^n\). This is motivated by the fact that the categories \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) are defined in terms of \(SL_2\). Only the special case \(\operatorname {Ver}_p\) has thus far been defined via \(C_p\) as well. Concretely, \(\operatorname {Ver}_p\) is both the semisimplification of \(\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2\) and of \(\operatorname {Rep}C_p\), and the latter definition is the one needed for Equation (1.1).

Choose a faithful two-dimensional \(C_p^n\)-representation V (in other words, an embedding of \(C_p^n\) into \(SL_2\)) and let \(\mathcal {D}\) be the additive monoidal subcategory it generates. We identify an explicit tensor ideal \(\mathcal {K}\) in \(\mathcal {D}\), and show in Sect. 5.3.5 (see also Remark 5.3.9(1)):

Theorem B

\(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) is the monoidal abelian envelope of the quotient category \(\mathcal {D}/\mathcal {K}\).

This generalises the definition of \(\operatorname {Ver}_p\) used in the construction of \(\operatorname {Fr}\) in Equation (1.1), and relates higher Verlinde categories to modular representations of elementary abelian p-groups, too. Indeed, in case \(n=1\), we find \(\mathcal {D}=\operatorname {Rep}C_p\) and \(\mathcal {K}\) is the tensor ideal of negligible morphisms, so that \(\mathcal {D}/\mathcal {K}=\operatorname {Ver}_p\).

Using an embedding \(C_p^n<S_{p^n}\) this then allows us to define, in Sect. 5.4, functors

$$\begin{aligned} \Phi ^V_\mathcal {C}:\mathcal {C}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n} \end{aligned}$$

generalising the construction of the Frobenius functor in Equation (1.1) for \(n=1\).

Based on the known cases for \(n=1\), which corresponds to the main theorem of [9], and our partial results for the case \(p^n=4\) (as explained below), we formulate the following conjecture (the first part is Conjecture 5.4.2(3), the second part for \(p^n=4\) is Conjecture 7.3.1):

Conjecture C

The functors \(\Phi ^V_\mathcal {C}\) define an \(\textbf{O}_n\)-functor. For certain natural choices of V, it detects fibering over \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\).

1.3 Connection with modular representations of elementary p -groups

We show that the part of Conjecture C predicting that the family of functors \(\Phi ^V_\mathcal {C}\) define an \(\textbf{O}_n\)-functor would follow from an intriguing conjecture about elementary abelian p-groups that can be stated without any reference to tensor categories. Let \(V\in \operatorname {Rep}C_p^n\) again be any faithful two-dimensional representation. We prove that the above monoidal subcategory \(\mathcal {D}\) of \(\operatorname {Rep}C_p^n\) has finitely many indecomposables up to isomorphism (i.e. V is algebraic) and that it has a minimal non-empty thick tensor ideal \(I\subset \mathcal {D}\).

Based on the case \(n=1\), where this can be seen immediately, the case \(p^n=4\), where it follows from the known classification of indecomposable modules for \(C_2^2\), and some evidence in the general case that we derive in forthcoming work, we formulate a second conjecture in Conjecture 5.4.2(1):

Conjecture D

The full subcategory \(I\subset \mathcal {D}\subset \operatorname {Rep}C_p^n\) remains a thick tensor ideal when considered in \(\operatorname {Rep}C_p^n\).

We then show in Theorem 5.4.3:

Theorem E

Conjecture D implies that the \(\Phi ^V_\mathcal {C}\) define an \(\textbf{O}_n\)-functor (i.e., the first part of Conjecture C).

1.4 The case \(p^n=4\)

In this case we can prove Conjecture D and partially also Conjecture C. From Theorem E, we obtain \(\textbf{O}_2\)-functors

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {C}\;\rightarrow \;\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{4}. \end{aligned}$$
(1.3)

We prove that, for two (Galois conjugate) choices of V, the functor in Equation (1.3) is exact for \(\mathcal {C}=\operatorname {Ver}_4\) and hence is exact on every tensor category that fibres over \(\operatorname {Ver}_4\). We make some progress towards proving that, for these choices of V, the functor in Equation (1.3) being exact on \(\mathcal {C}\) is also a sufficient condition for \(\mathcal {C}\) to fibre over \(\operatorname {Ver}_4\). In particular, we show in Theorem 7.3.3:

Theorem F

Assuming [2, Conjecture 1.4], the constructed \(\textbf{O}_2\)-functor detects fibering over \(\operatorname {Ver}_4\) at least for finite tensor categories.

In this case we also derive a large family of new \(\textbf{O}_1\)-functors based on the fourth tensor power. Again under [2, Conjecture 1.4] these should, at least on finite tensor categories, all single out (via the exactness condition) tannakian categories. Our analysis also leads to unconditional results, for instance the following result in Corollary 7.2.3:

Theorem G

Consider \(n>2\). For any two projective objects P, Q in \(\operatorname {Ver}_{2^n}\) or \(\operatorname {Ver}_{2^n}^+\), the space \(\operatorname {Hom}(P,Q^{\otimes 4})\), viewed as a representation over the Klein 4-subgroup \(C_2^2<S_4\), is a direct sum of non-trivial permutation modules.

1.5 Structure of the paper

In Sect. 2 we recall some required background. In Sect. 3 we explain some properties of the Deligne tensor product that are known but not always easy to locate in the literature. In Sect. 4 we introduce and develop the theory of \(\textbf{O}\)-functors. In Sect. 5 we introduce a conjectural \(\textbf{O}\)-functor corresponding to each \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\). In Sect. 6 we classify linear symmetric monoidal functors from \(\operatorname {Rep}_{\Bbbk } C_2^2\), for \(\textrm{char}(\Bbbk )=2\), to tensor categories, leading to a large family of \(\textbf{O}\)-functors, including the main ‘conjectural one’ from Sect. 5 for \(\operatorname {Ver}_4\). In Sect. 7 we describe which tensor categories the above \(\textbf{O}\)-functors single out via their exactness condition.

2 Preliminaries

Throughout, \(\Bbbk \) will denote an algebraically closed field, usually of characteristic \(p>0\). Then we have the Frobenius automorphism

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {Frob}:\,\Bbbk \rightarrow \Bbbk \,,\; \lambda \mapsto \lambda ^p. \end{aligned}$$

We consider the symmetric group \(S_n\) as the permutation group of the set \(\{1,2,\dots , n\}.\)

We set \(\mathbb {N}:=\{0,1,\dots \}\).

2.1 Tensor categories and functors

We refer to [16] for basic notions regarding monoidal categories.

2.1.1

We will abbreviate ‘\(\Bbbk \)-linear symmetric monoidal category’ to \(\Bbbk \)-LSM category, leaving out \(\Bbbk \) when it is clear from context. It is understood that the tensor product in such a category is \(\Bbbk \)-linear in each variable. Similarly, we speak of LSM functors between LSM categories.

More generally, for \(\Bbbk _i\)-LSM categories \(\mathcal {C}_i\), \(i\in \{1,2\}\) and a field homomorphism \(\varphi :\Bbbk _1\rightarrow \Bbbk _2\), a \(\varphi \)-LSM functor \(F:\mathcal {C}_1\rightarrow \mathcal {C}_2\) is a symmetric monoidal functor F such that

$$\begin{aligned} F(\lambda f)=\varphi (\lambda )F(f),\quad \text{ for } \text{ all } \lambda \in \Bbbk _1, \end{aligned}$$

and all morphisms f in \(\mathcal {C}_1\).

Usually, this situation will occur for \(\Bbbk _1=\Bbbk _2=\Bbbk \) and \(\varphi \) a power of \(\operatorname {Frob}\).

2.1.2

A \(\Bbbk \)-LSM category \((\mathcal {C},\otimes ,\textbf{1})\) is a tensor category over \(\Bbbk \) if

  1. (1)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) is abelian with objects of finite length;

  2. (2)

    \(\Bbbk \rightarrow \operatorname {End}_{\mathcal {C}}(\textbf{1})\) is an isomorphism;

  3. (3)

    \((\mathcal {C},\otimes ,\textbf{1})\) is rigid, meaning that every object X has a monoidal dual \(X^\vee \).

Such categories are also sometimes called symmetric tensor categories or pretannakian categories. Note that \(\textbf{1}\) is a simple object, see [16, Theorem 4.3.8]. It then follows from the assumptions (1)-(3) that morphism spaces in a tensor category are finite-dimensional.

The first example of a tensor category is the category \(\textrm{Vec}=\textrm{Vec}_{\Bbbk }\) of finite-dimensional vector spaces over \(\Bbbk \). We denote the category of all vector spaces by \(\textrm{Vec}^\infty \).

For tensor categories, we will usually leave out the reference ‘over \(\Bbbk \)’ when it is clear from context over which field we work.

A \(\varphi \)-tensor functor is an exact \(\varphi \)-LSM functor between tensor categories over the source and target of a field homomorphism \(\varphi \). We leave out reference to \(\varphi \) when \(\varphi =\operatorname {id}\).

A tensor subcategory of a tensor category is a full subcategory which is closed under taking subquotients, tensor products and duals. A tensor functor \(F:\mathcal {C}_1\rightarrow \mathcal {C}_2\) is called surjective if every object in \(\mathcal {C}_2\) is a subquotient of one in the essential image of F. In other words, there is no proper tensor subcategory of \(\mathcal {C}_2\) in which F takes values.

Example 2.1.3

  1. (1)

    For an abstract group H, we have the tensor category \(\operatorname {Rep}_{\Bbbk }H=\operatorname {Rep}H\) of finite-dimensional representations.

  2. (2)

    For an affine group scheme G over \(\Bbbk \), we have the tensor category \(\operatorname {Rep}_{\Bbbk }G=\operatorname {Rep}G\) of rational representations (comodules over the coordinate ring). In particular, we have a (forgetful) tensor functor

    $$ \operatorname {Rep}_\Bbbk G \rightarrow \operatorname {Rep}_\Bbbk G(\Bbbk ). $$

2.1.4

Following [16, Chapter 6], we say that a tensor category is finite, if it has enough projective objects and only finitely many simple objects up to isomorphism. This is equivalent to demanding that the underlying abelian category is equivalent to the category of finite-dimensional modules of a finite-dimensional associative \(\Bbbk \)-algebra.

Note also that in a tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\), the existence of one (non-zero) projective object implies that \(\mathcal {C}\) has enough projective objects; and projective objects are injective.

We record some weaker ‘finiteness’ conditions on tensor categories:

  1. (S)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) is a union of tensor (sub)categories with finitely many simple objects, up to isomorphism;

  2. (P)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) is a union of tensor categories which have enough projective objects (or equivalently, which have non-zero projective objects);

  3. (SP)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) satisfies (S) and (P), or equivalently, it is a union of finite tensor categories.

Note that these three properties are inherited by tensor subcategories. On tensor categories satisfying (S), we have a well-defined notion of Frobenius–Perron dimension \(\operatorname {FPdim}\) by [16, Proposition 4.5.7].

An example of a tensor category satisfying (SP) is \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^\infty }\).

Another finiteness condition that we can impose extends the notion of algebraic representations due to Alperin. Concretely, we say that an object in a tensor category is algebraic if there are only finitely many indecomposable summands (up to isomorphism) in its tensor powers. Equivalently, an object is algebraic if its image in the split Grothendieck ring satisfies a polynomial equation.

2.1.5

A tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\) is of moderate growth, see [1, 9, 10], if for every \(X\in \mathcal {C}\), the limit (the growth dimension of X)

$$\begin{aligned} \lim _{n\rightarrow \infty }\root n \of {\ell (X^{\otimes n})}\;\in \;\mathbb {R}_{\ge 0}\cup \{\infty \} \end{aligned}$$

is finite, see [9, §4], where \(\ell \) denotes the length of an object.

It follows from the alternative characterisation in [9, Lemma 4.11(3)] that if \(\mathcal {C}\) is of moderate growth and there exists a surjective tensor functor \(F:\mathcal {C}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}'\), then also \(\mathcal {C}'\) is of moderate growth. Tensor categories satisfying (S) are of moderate growth, since \(\ell (X)\le \operatorname {FPdim}(X)\) and the Frobenius–Perron dimension is multiplicative.

2.2 Exactness criteria

We will be particularly interested in LSM functors between tensor categories that are not (necessarily) exact.

The following property, see [11, Theorem 2.4.1] or [7], will be used often.

Theorem 2.2.1

Let \(F:\mathcal {C}_1\rightarrow \mathcal {C}_2\) be a \(\varphi \)-LSM functor between tensor categories over fields \(\Bbbk _1,\Bbbk _2\). Then F is exact (i.e. a \(\varphi \)-tensor functor) if and only if it is faithful.

Lemma 2.2.2

Consider a \(\varphi \)-LSM functor \(F:\mathcal {C}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}'\) between tensor categories, where \(\mathcal {C}\) satisfies (P). The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    F is exact.

  2. (2)

    F is faithful.

  3. (3)

    There are tensor subcategories \(\{\mathcal {C}_\alpha \subset \mathcal {C}\}\) satisfying \(\cup _\alpha \mathcal {C}_\alpha =\mathcal {C}\), with projective objects \(P_\alpha \in \mathcal {C}_\alpha \) such that \(F(P_\alpha )\not =0\).

Proof

That (1) and (2) are equivalent is Theorem 2.2.1. Clearly (2) implies (3). Since tensoring with a projective object splits every short exact sequence, it follows that (3) implies (1). \(\square \)

Corollary 2.2.3

Consider a surjective \(\varphi \)-tensor functor \(F:\mathcal {C}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}'\) between finite tensor categories and a \(\varphi '\)-LSM functor \(F':\mathcal {C}'\rightarrow \mathcal {C}''\) to a third tensor category such that the composite \(F'\circ F\) is exact. Then \(F'\) is a \(\varphi '\)-tensor functor.

Proof

This follows from the equivalence between (1) and (2) in Lemma 2.2.2 and the observation, see [16, Theorem 6.1.16], that F sends projective objects in \(\mathcal {C}\) to projective objects in \(\mathcal {C}'\). \(\square \)

2.2.4

As recalled in Theorem 2.2.1, an LSM functor between tensor categories is not exact if and only if its kernel is a non-trivial tensor ideal. In general for an LSM category \(\mathcal {A}\) and a tensor ideal I in \(\mathcal {A}\) it will be understood that \(\mathcal {A}\rightarrow \mathcal {A}/I\) stands for the LSM functor which sends every object to itself and every morphism to its equivalence class. An important example, for any tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\), is the semisimplification

$$\begin{aligned} \Sigma : \mathcal {C}\rightarrow \overline{\mathcal {C}}, \end{aligned}$$

see [18] for an overview. Most importantly, \(\overline{\mathcal {C}}\) is the quotient with respect to the unique maximal tensor ideal and is again a tensor category, and moreover semisimple.

For a finite group G, the minimal non-zero tensor ideal in \(\operatorname {Rep}_{\Bbbk } G\) (say over a field \(\Bbbk \) such that \(\textrm{char}(\Bbbk )\) divides |G|) is the ideal of all morphisms that factor through projective objects. The resulting quotient is the stable category \(\operatorname {Stab}G\).

2.3 Incompressible categories

An incompressible (tensor) category, see [10] and references therein, is a tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\) for which every tensor functor \(\mathcal {C}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}'\) realises an equivalence with a tensor subcategory of \(\mathcal {C}'\).

In this section, we assume that \(\operatorname {char}(\Bbbk )=p>0\). The list of currently known incompressible tensor categories is given in [2]. We review some essential properties and conjectures concerning these.

2.3.1

Recall from Example 2.1.3 that \(\operatorname {Rep}_{\Bbbk } SL_2\) is the category of finite-dimensional rational \(SL_2(\Bbbk )\)-representations. The full subcategory of \(\operatorname {Rep}_{\Bbbk }SL_2\) of tilting modules, see [20, Chapter E], is denoted by \(\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2\). This is also the full monoidal subcategory comprising direct summands of direct sums of tensor powers of the natural (2-dimensional) representation V. Indecomposable tilting modules are labelled by their highest weight, and we denote them as \(T_i\), \(i\in \mathbb {N}\). For instance, \(T_0\simeq \textbf{1}\) and \(T_1\simeq V\).

By [4, Theorem 5.3.1], the proper tensor ideals in \(\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2\) form one countable chain

$$\begin{aligned} I_1\supset I_2\supset I_3\supset \cdots , \end{aligned}$$

with \(I_n\) the ideal generated by the Steinberg module \(St_n=T_{p^n-1}\). More precisely, \(I_n\) comprises all morphisms that factor through a direct sum of \(T_j\) with \(j\ge p^n-1\). Furthermore,

$$\begin{aligned} I_n(T_i,T_j)\;=\;0 \end{aligned}$$

unless \(i+j> 2p^n-2\). In particular, if we denote by \(\operatorname {Tilt}^nSL_2\), for \(n\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\) the full subcategory of \(\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2\) comprising direct sums of copies of \(T_i,i<p^n-1\), then the composite

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {Tilt}^n SL_2\;\hookrightarrow \; \operatorname {Tilt}SL_2\;\rightarrow \; (\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2)/I_n \end{aligned}$$

is fully faithful. We denote further by \(\operatorname {Tilt}^{[n]}SL_2\), for \(n\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\) the full subcategory of \(\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2\) comprising direct sums of copies of \(T_i\) with \(p^{n-1}-1\le i<p^n\).

2.3.2

By [2, 6], for each \(n\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\), the LSM category \((\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2)/I_n\) admits a ‘monoidal abelian envelope’. Concretely, for each \(n\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\) we have an LSM-functor

$$\begin{aligned} \Sigma ^n:\;\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2\rightarrow \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n} \end{aligned}$$

with kernel \(I_n\), to a tensor category \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\). Note that \(\Sigma ^1\) corresponds to the semisimplification of the (non-abelian) symmetric monoidal category \(\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2\). We will use the same notation for the corresponding faithful LSM-functor

$$\begin{aligned} \Sigma ^n:\;(\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2)/I_n\rightarrow \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}. \end{aligned}$$
(2.1)

Moreover, \(\Sigma ^n\) restricts to an equivalence

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {Tilt}SL_2\supset \operatorname {Tilt}^{[n]}SL_2\;\xrightarrow {\sim }\; \mathcal {P}\subset \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n} \end{aligned}$$
(2.2)

with the category \(\mathcal {P}\) of projective objects in \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\), see [2, Theorem 4.5].

It is also proved in [2, 6] that, for each tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\), restriction along \(\Sigma ^n\) in Equation (2.1) gives an equivalence between the category of tensor functors \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\) and the category of faithful LSM functors \((\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2)/I_n\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\).

2.3.3

It is proved in [2] that each \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) is incompressible and that the simple objects in \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) are labelled by

$$\begin{aligned} \{L_i^{[n]}\mid 0\le i\le p^{n-1}(p-1)-1\} \end{aligned}$$

such that

$$\begin{aligned} L_0^{[n]}\simeq \textbf{1},\quad L_1^{[n]}\simeq \Sigma ^n(T_1)=\Sigma ^n(V), \quad \text{ and }\quad L^{[n]}_{p^{n-1}(p-2)}=\bar{\textbf{1}}, \end{aligned}$$

where the last example assumes \(p>2\) and denotes by \(\bar{\textbf{1}}\) the odd line in the category \(\textrm{sVec}\) of supervector spaces. When no confusion is possible, we will write \(L_i\) instead of \(L_i^{[n]}\). However, we have inclusions \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\subset \operatorname {Ver}_{p^{n+1}}\) which identify \(L_i^{[n]}\) with \(L_{pi}^{[n+1]}\).

We will also refer to the subcategories \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}^+\subset \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) from [2, §4.1]. The tensor category \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}^+\) is a direct summand of \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) that contains half of the simple objects and corresponds to the \(SL_2\)-tilting modules with even highest weight under (2.2). Moreover, \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\simeq \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}^+\boxtimes \textrm{sVec}\) if \(p>2\). We will be particularly interested in \(\operatorname {Ver}_4^+\) and \(\operatorname {Ver}_4\), described as \(\mathcal {C}_1\) and \(\mathcal {C}_2\) in [1].

The following theorem is due to the first author, Etingof and Ostrik, see [9, Theorem 1.1]. Special cases were obtained earlier in for instance [15, 17, 22]. For the notion of Frobenius exactness we refer to [9, 17], or [5, Theorem C] or Example 4.1.5(2) and Example 5.2.2 below.

Theorem 2.3.4

(\(\operatorname {Ver}_p\)-Theorem) The following conditions are equivalent on a tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\):

  1. (1)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) is of moderate growth and Frobenius exact;

  2. (2)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) admits a tensor functor to \(\operatorname {Ver}_p\).

Moreover, the tensor functor in (2) is unique up to isomorphism.

This is to be compared with the following conjecture due to Benson, Etingof and Ostrik, see [2, Conjecture 1.4].

Conjecture 2.3.5

(\(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^\infty }\)-Conjecture) The following conditions are equivalent on a tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\):

  1. (1)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) is of moderate growth;

  2. (2)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) admits a tensor functor to \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^\infty }\).

We conclude the preliminaries with some considerations regarding exactness of LSM functors out of our incompressible categories. We fix \(n\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\) and \(i\in \mathbb {Z}\). The Frobenius–Perron dimensions of all simple objects in \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) have been calculated in [2, Corollary 4.44]. We use the result freely in the following two proofs.

Lemma 2.3.6

Assume \(p^n>2\). Consider a field homomorphism \(\varphi :\Bbbk \rightarrow \Bbbk '\). A \(\varphi \)-LSM functor \(F:\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\) to a finite tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\) over \(\Bbbk '\) is exact if and only if

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {FPdim}(F(L_1))\;=\; \operatorname {FPdim}(L_1)\;=\; 2\cos \left( \frac{\pi }{p^n}\right) , \end{aligned}$$

which is the case if and only if \(\operatorname {FPdim}(F(L_1))\not \in \{2\cos (\frac{\pi }{p^m}):m<n\}\).

Proof

In case F is exact, it preserves Frobenius–Perron dimension as a consequence of [16, Proposition 3.3.13]. Consider the LSM functors

$$\begin{aligned} (\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2)/ I_n\;\xrightarrow {\Sigma ^n}\;\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\;\xrightarrow {F}\;\mathcal {C}. \end{aligned}$$

Assume that F is not exact. Then Lemma 2.2.2 and the fact that all projective objects in \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) are in the essential image of \(\Sigma ^n\) imply that \(F\circ \Sigma ^n\) is not faithful. Hence, \(F\circ \Sigma ^n\) factors via \((\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2)/ I_m\) for \(m<n\). We take the minimal such m. By the abelian envelope property of Sect. 2.3.2, it follows that \(F\circ \Sigma ^n\) is also the composite of LSM functors

$$\begin{aligned} (\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2)/ I_n\;\twoheadrightarrow \;(\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2)/ I_m\;\xrightarrow {\Sigma ^m}\;\operatorname {Ver}_{p^m}\;\rightarrow \;\mathcal {C}, \end{aligned}$$

where the right-most functor is exact. By the first paragraph we find that

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {FPdim}(F(L_1))\;=\; 2\cos \left( \frac{\pi }{p^m}\right) \;<\; 2\cos \left( \frac{\pi }{p^n}\right) , \end{aligned}$$

concluding the proof. \(\square \)

We refer to the next section, and references therein, for a full treatment of the Deligne tensor product \(\boxtimes \) appearing in the next corollary.

Corollary 2.3.7

Assume \(p^n>2\). A \(\operatorname {Frob}^i\)-LSM functor

$$\begin{aligned} F:\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\rightarrow \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n} \end{aligned}$$

is exact if and only if we are in one of the following cases:

  1. (1)

    \(F(L_1)=\textbf{1}\boxtimes L_1\), or \(F(L_1)=\bar{\textbf{1}}\boxtimes (\bar{\textbf{1}}\otimes L_1)\) if \(p>2\), yielding equivalences

    $$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\xrightarrow {\sim }\textrm{Vec}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\quad \text{ or }\quad \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\xrightarrow {\sim }\textrm{sVec}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}^+. \end{aligned}$$
  2. (2)

    \(F(L_1)= L_1\boxtimes \textbf{1}\), or \(F(L_1)=(\bar{\textbf{1}}\otimes L_1)\boxtimes \bar{\textbf{1}}\) if \(p>2\), yielding similar equivalences.

Remark 2.3.8

There exists a \(\operatorname {Frob}\)-LSM auto-equivalence (i.e. a \(\operatorname {Frob}\)-tensor auto-equivalence) of \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\). Indeed, for a \(\Bbbk \)-LSM category \(\mathcal {A}\), denote by \(\mathcal {A}^{(1)}\) the same pre-additive symmetric monoidal category, but with a new \(\Bbbk \)-linear structure where the new action of \(\lambda \in \Bbbk \) on a morphism f is given by \(\lambda ^p f\) in terms of the old linear structure. Then \(\mathcal {A}^{(1)}\) is again a \(\Bbbk \)-LSM category, a priori different from \(\mathcal {A}\). We can thus reformulate the claim as saying that \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) and \((\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n})^{(1)}\) are actually equivalent as tensor categories over \(\Bbbk \). Now \(\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2\) and \((\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2)^{(1)}\) are equivalent, for instance because \(SL_2\) can be defined over \(\mathbb {F}_p\), or by using the equivalence with the diagrammatic Temperley–Lieb category, and this equivalence exchanges the ideals \(I_n\). We can then realise \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) and \((\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n})^{(1)}\) as the abelian envelopes of the equivalent categories \((\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2)/I_n\) and \(((\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2)/I_n)^{(1)}\).

3 Deligne products

In this section, we do not claim originality. We write out some useful aspects of the Deligne tensor product as first introduced in [12]. Many of these have appeared implicitly in [5, 9, 17], but not always in full detail or with complete proof. Recall that \(\Bbbk \) is an algebraically closed field.

3.1 Comodules of coalgebras

3.1.1

For a coalgebra C over \(\Bbbk \), we consider the categories of finite-dimensional, and all, left comodules, respectively:

$$\begin{aligned} \textrm{Comod}_{C}\quad \text{ and }\quad \textrm{Comod}^\infty _{C}\simeq \operatorname {Ind}(\textrm{Comod}_{C}). \end{aligned}$$

For a right C-comodule M and a left C-comodule N we have the cotensor product

$$\begin{aligned} M\Box ^C N\;=\; \textrm{Eq}(M\otimes _{\Bbbk }N\rightrightarrows M\otimes _{\Bbbk }C\otimes _{\Bbbk }N), \end{aligned}$$

which is a vector space. The following lemma is well-known.

Lemma 3.1.2

  1. (1)

    A right C-comodule M is coflat (\(M\Box ^C-\) is exact) if and only if it is injective.

  2. (2)

    For coalgebras \(C_1,C_2\), consider a right \(C_1\otimes C_2\)-comodule T for which

    $$\begin{aligned} \textrm{Comod}_{C_1}\times \textrm{Comod}_{C_2}\,\rightarrow \, \textrm{Vec}^\infty ,\;\, (M_1,M_2)\mapsto T\Box ^{C_1\otimes C_2}(M_1\otimes M_2) \end{aligned}$$

    is exact in both variables. Then T is injective over \(C_1\otimes C_2\).

  3. (3)

    For coalgebras \(C_1,C_2\), the assignment which sends a \((C_2,C_1)\)-bicomodule M to the functor

    $$\begin{aligned} M\Box ^{C_1}-:\; \textrm{Comod}_{C_1}\rightarrow \textrm{Comod}_{C_2}^\infty \end{aligned}$$

    yields an equivalence between the category of right injective bicomodules and the category of exact \(\Bbbk \)-linear functors.

Proof

For part (1) it suffices to observe that

$$\begin{aligned} M\Box ^C-\;\simeq \;\operatorname {Hom}_{C}(-^*, M) \end{aligned}$$

as functors from \(\textrm{Comod}_{C}\) to \(\textrm{Vec}^\infty \), where we interpret the dual space of a finite-dimensional left C-comodule canonically as a right C-comodule.

For part (2), it is sufficient to show that T is coflat, by part (1). This is a straightforward generalisation of [12, Proposition 5.7]. We can express the coflatness as vanishing of a first derived functor; and it is sufficient to prove vanishing when evaluated on simple comodules, since the cohomology functors commute with direct limits and are exact in the middle.

Now, the simple \(C_1\otimes C_2\)-comodules are precisely those of the form \(V_1\otimes V_2\) for simple \(C_i\)-comodules \(V_i\). This is true because \(\Bbbk \) is algebraically closed, see for instance [12, Lemme 5.9].

However, vanishing of the cohomology functor on \(C_1\otimes C_2\)-comodules that are of the exterior tensor product form \(V_1\otimes V_2\) follows from the assumptions.

Part (3) is standard, using part (1). \(\square \)

3.2 The Deligne product of abelian categories

Let \(\mathcal {A}\) and \(\mathcal {B}\) be two essentially small \(\Bbbk \)-linear abelian categories.

3.2.1

The Deligne tensor product \(\mathcal {A}\boxtimes \mathcal {B}=\mathcal {A}\boxtimes _{\Bbbk }\mathcal {B}\) (if it exists) is a \(\Bbbk \)-linear abelian category, equipped with a bilinear bifunctor

$$\begin{aligned} -\boxtimes -:\;\mathcal {A}\times \mathcal {B}\rightarrow \mathcal {A}\boxtimes \mathcal {B}, \quad (X,Y)\mapsto X\boxtimes Y, \end{aligned}$$
(3.1)

satisfying the following universal property. For every \(\Bbbk \)-linear abelian category \(\mathcal {C}\), restriction along Equation (3.1) yields an equivalence between the category of right exact \(\Bbbk \)-linear functors \(\mathcal {A}\boxtimes \mathcal {B}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\) with the category of bilinear bifunctors \(\mathcal {A}\times \mathcal {B}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\) that are right exact in each variable.

As demonstrated in [21], the Deligne tensor product need not always exist. Of course, when \(\mathcal {A}\boxtimes \mathcal {B}\) exists, it is unique up to equivalence.

3.2.2

Keeping the set-up of Sect. 3.2.1, assume now that all morphisms spaces in \(\mathcal {A}\) are finite-dimensional and all objects have finite length. It then follows from Takeuchi’s theorem, see [23] or [16, Theorem 1.9.15], that there exists a faithful exact \(\Bbbk \)-linear functor \(\omega :\mathcal {A}\rightarrow \textrm{Vec}\), which allows us to identify \(\mathcal {A}\) with the category of finite-dimensional comodules of the coalgebra

$$\begin{aligned} C\;=\;\int ^{X\in \mathcal {A}}\omega (X)^*\otimes _{\Bbbk }\omega (X). \end{aligned}$$

We define the (abelian) category \(\textrm{Comod}_C(\mathcal {B})\) of (left) C-comodules in \(\mathcal {B}\) as the category of objects Y in \(\mathcal {B}\), equipped with an algebra morphism

$$\begin{aligned} C_Y^*\;\rightarrow \; \operatorname {End}_{\mathcal {B}}(Y), \end{aligned}$$

for some finite-dimensional subcoalgebra \(C_Y\subset C\). Here we use the fact that a coalgebra is the union of its finite-dimensional subcoalgebras, allowing us to avoid using the ind-completion of \(\mathcal {B}\) in the definition. We have an obvious bilinear bifunctor

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {A}\times \mathcal {B}\;\rightarrow \; \textrm{Comod}_C\mathcal {B}. \end{aligned}$$

The following lemma is a minor generalisation of [21, Theorem 3] (in the sense that no finiteness assumptions are made on \(\mathcal {B}\)), but more importantly includes the explicit realisation of the Deligne product that we need.

Lemma 3.2.3

Under the assumption on \(\mathcal {A}\) in Sect. 3.2.2 and with the corresponding C as defined there, we have:

  1. (1)

    The Deligne product \(\mathcal {A}\boxtimes \mathcal {B}\) exists and is given by \(\textrm{Comod}_C\mathcal {B}\).

  2. (2)

    Every object in \(\mathcal {A}\boxtimes \mathcal {B}\) is a quotient of one of the form \(X\boxtimes Y\).

  3. (3)

    Every object in \(\mathcal {A}\boxtimes \mathcal {B}\) is a subobject of one of the form \(X\boxtimes Y\).

Proof

By the general theory of [21], for instance Remark 10 and Theorem 18, we need to show that \(\textrm{Comod}_C\mathcal {B}\) is equivalent to the category of compact (finitely presented) objects in the category of bilinear bifunctors

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {A}^{\textrm{op}}\times \mathcal {B}^{\textrm{op}}\;\rightarrow \;\textrm{Vec}^\infty \end{aligned}$$

that are left exact in each variable. The latter category can be reinterpreted as the category of linear left exact functors from \(\mathcal {B}^{\textrm{op}}\) to

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {Ind}\mathcal {A}\;\simeq \;\textrm{Comod}^\infty _C, \end{aligned}$$

the category of all (not necessarily finite-dimensional) C-comodules over \(\Bbbk \). Using the forgetful functor from \(\textrm{Comod}^\infty _C\) to \(\textrm{Vec}^\infty \), we can observe that we can reinterpret (left exact) functors from \(\mathcal {B}^\textrm{op}\) to \(\textrm{Comod}^\infty _C\) as (left exact) functors from \(\mathcal {B}^\textrm{op}\) to \(\textrm{Vec}^\infty \) equipped with a C-comodule structure. In conclusion, we have identified our original functor category with the category of C-comodules in \(\operatorname {Ind}\mathcal {B}\) (in the ordinary sense, meaning objects \(Y\in \operatorname {Ind}\mathcal {B}\) with a coaction \(Y\rightarrow C\otimes _{\Bbbk }Y\)). Its subcategory of compact objects is indeed \(\textrm{Comod}_C(\mathcal {B})\): To show that compact C-comodules in \(\operatorname {Ind}\mathcal {B}\) must have their underlying object in \(\mathcal {B}\), it suffices to test against comodules of the form \(C\otimes _{\Bbbk }(\textrm{colim} Y_i)\) with \(Y_i\in \mathcal {B}\). To see that the underlying object being in \(\mathcal {B}\) is sufficient to be compact for a C-comodule in \(\operatorname {Ind}\mathcal {B}\) one can realise C-linear morphisms spaces as equalisers of \(\mathcal {B}\)-morphism spaces. This concludes the proof of part (1).

For M in \(\textrm{Comod}_C\mathcal {B}\) realised as \(C_{M_0}^*\rightarrow \operatorname {End}_{\mathcal {B}}(M_0)\), with \(M_0\in \mathcal {B}\),

$$\begin{aligned} M\;\hookrightarrow \; C_{M_0}\boxtimes M_0\quad \text{ and }\quad C_{M_0}^*\boxtimes {M_0}\;\twoheadrightarrow \; M \end{aligned}$$

are an obvious monomorphism and epimorphism proving parts (2) and (3). \(\square \)

Example 3.2.4

  1. (1)

    For a finite group G and a \(\Bbbk \)-linear abelian category \(\mathcal {B}\),

    $$\begin{aligned} \textrm{Comod}_{(\Bbbk G)^*}\mathcal {B}\;\simeq \; (\operatorname {Rep}G)\boxtimes \mathcal {B}\;\simeq \; \mathcal {B}\boxtimes (\operatorname {Rep}G)\;\simeq \;\operatorname {Fun}(BG,\mathcal {B}) \end{aligned}$$

    is the category of G-representations in \(\mathcal {B}\).

  2. (2)

    More generally, assume that \(\mathcal {A}\) is a finite category in the sense of [16], meaning it is equivalent to the category of finite-dimensional modules over a finite-dimensional associative algebra A. Then we can simplify all the above constructions by replacing the (now finite-dimensional) coalgebra C by its dual algebra \(C^*=A\simeq \operatorname {End}(\omega )\) (for \(\omega :\mathcal {A}\rightarrow \textrm{Vec}\) as above). So \(\mathcal {A}\boxtimes \mathcal {B}\) is the category of A-modules in \(\mathcal {B}\).

  3. (3)

    Yet equivalently, for \(\mathcal {A}\) as in (2), we have

    $$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {A}\boxtimes \mathcal {B}\simeq \operatorname {Fun}_{\Bbbk }(\mathcal {P}^{\textrm{op}},\mathcal {B}), \end{aligned}$$

    with \(\mathcal {P}\) the category of projective objects in \(\mathcal {A}\).

3.2.5

Denote by \(\mathcal {A}b\mathcal {C}at_{\Bbbk }\) the 2-category whose objects are essentially small \(\Bbbk \)-linear categories, 1-morphisms are \(\Bbbk \)-linear (not necessarily exact) functors and 2-morphisms are all natural transformations. We denote the full 2-subcategory \(\mathcal {T}ak_{\Bbbk }\) (after Takeuchi) of \(\Bbbk \)-linear abelian categories with objects of finite length and morphism spaces that are finite-dimensional. We consider 2-subcategories

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {A}b\mathcal {C}at^{ex}_{\Bbbk }\subset \mathcal {A}b\mathcal {C}at^{rex}_{\Bbbk }\subset \mathcal {A}b\mathcal {C}at_{\Bbbk }\quad \text{ and }\quad \mathcal {T}ak^{ex}_{\Bbbk }\subset \mathcal {T}ak^{rex}_{\Bbbk }\subset \mathcal {T}ak_{\Bbbk } \end{aligned}$$

by keeping the same objects but restricting the 1-morphisms to (right) exact functors.

The Deligne product naturally leads to the notion of a pseudo-functor (a non-strict 2-functor). Indeed, assuming the relevant Deligne products exist, for right exact functors \(F_1:\mathcal {A}_1\rightarrow \mathcal {A}_2\) and \(G_1:\mathcal {B}_1\rightarrow \mathcal {B}_2\), we obtain an isomorphism class of right exact functors \(F_1\boxtimes G_1:\mathcal {A}_1\boxtimes \mathcal {A}_2\rightarrow \mathcal {B}_1\boxtimes \mathcal {B}_2\), by applying the definition to the bifunctor \(\mathcal {A}_1\times \mathcal {B}_1\rightarrow \mathcal {A}_2\times \mathcal {B}_2\rightarrow \mathcal {A}_2\boxtimes \mathcal {B}_2\), obtained also from the definition of the Deligne product. There is no guarantee that we can choose representatives to have \((F_2\boxtimes G_2)\circ (F_1\boxtimes G_1)=(F_2\circ F_1)\boxtimes (G_2\circ G_1)\).

Proposition 3.2.6

There is a pseudo-functor

$$\begin{aligned} -\boxtimes -:\;\mathcal {T}ak_{\Bbbk }^{ex}\times \mathcal {A}b\mathcal {C}at_{\Bbbk }\;\rightarrow \; \mathcal {A}b\mathcal {C}at_{\Bbbk } \end{aligned}$$

that agrees with the pseudo-functor (implicit in the definition of \(\boxtimes \))

$$\begin{aligned} -\boxtimes -:\;\mathcal {T}ak_{\Bbbk }^{rex}\times \mathcal {A}b\mathcal {C}at_{\Bbbk }^{rex}\;\rightarrow \; \mathcal {A}b\mathcal {C}at_{\Bbbk }^{rex} \end{aligned}$$

on \(\mathcal {T}ak^{ex}_{\Bbbk }\times \mathcal {A}b\mathcal {C}at^{rex}_{\Bbbk }\).

Proof

By the above, \(\mathcal {T}ak_{\Bbbk }^{ex}\) is equivalent to the 2-category \(\mathcal {C}o\mathcal {A}l\) which has as objects coalgebras over \(\Bbbk \), as 1-morphisms bicomodules that are injective as right comodules and as 2-morphisms the morphisms of bimodules. We can replace \(\mathcal {T}ak_{\Bbbk }^{ex}\) by \(\mathcal {C}o\mathcal {A}l\) for the purposes of the proposition.

For \(C\in \mathcal {C}o\mathcal {A}l\) and \(\mathcal {B}\in \mathcal {A}b\mathcal {C}at\) we then set (following Lemma 3.2.3(1))

$$\begin{aligned} C\boxtimes \mathcal {B}:= \textrm{Comod}_C\mathcal {B}. \end{aligned}$$

For all \(C_1,C_2\in \mathcal {C}o\mathcal {A}l\) and \(\mathcal {B}_1,\mathcal {B}_2\in \mathcal {A}b\mathcal {C}at\) we must now define a functor

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {C}o\mathcal {A}l(C_1,C_2)\times \mathcal {A}b\mathcal {C}at(\mathcal {B}_1,\mathcal {B}_2)\;\rightarrow \; \mathcal {A}b\mathcal {C}at(\textrm{Comod}_{C_1}\mathcal {B}_1,\textrm{Comod}_{C_2}\mathcal {B}_2). \end{aligned}$$

For \(M\in \mathcal {C}o\mathcal {A}l(C_1,C_2)\) and \(G\in \mathcal {A}b\mathcal {C}at(\mathcal {B}_1,\mathcal {B}_2)\), we define the composite functor

$$\begin{aligned} M\boxtimes G:\; \textrm{Comod}_{C_1}\mathcal {B}_1\xrightarrow {G} \textrm{Comod}_{C_1}\mathcal {B}_2\xrightarrow {M\Box ^{C_1}-} \textrm{Comod}_{C_2}\mathcal {B}_2, \end{aligned}$$

where we use the notation G for the canonical lift of G to the categories of comodules. Finally, for a morphism \(f:M\rightarrow M'\) and a natural transformation \(\beta : G\Rightarrow G'\), the corresponding natural transformation from \(M\boxtimes G\) to \(M'\boxtimes G'\) is easily defined.

That this definition satisfies all properties of a pseudo-functor and agrees with the classical interpretation of \(-\boxtimes -\) as a pseudo-functor is left as an exercise. \(\square \)

Remark 3.2.7

We cannot further extend \(-\boxtimes -\) to a pseudo-functor

$$\begin{aligned} -\boxtimes -:\;\mathcal {T}ak_{\Bbbk }^{rex}\times \mathcal {A}b\mathcal {C}at_{\Bbbk }\;\rightarrow \; \mathcal {A}b\mathcal {C}at_{\Bbbk }. \end{aligned}$$

Indeed, the functors \(H_0(G_1,-)\) and \(H^0(G_2,-)\) do not commute on \(G_1\times G_2\)-representations, for finite groups \(G_1,G_2\). Hence, there can be no functor ‘\(H_0(G_1,-)\boxtimes H^0(G_2,-)\)’ on the diagonal yielding two commutative triangles (up to isomorphism)

Corollary 3.2.8

Take \(\mathcal {A},\mathcal {B},\mathcal {B}'\) in \(\mathcal {T}ak\). For a \(\Bbbk \)-linear functor \(F:\mathcal {B}\rightarrow \mathcal {B}'\), the functor \(\mathcal {A}\boxtimes F\) is an equivalence if and only if F is an equivalence.

Proof

If F is an equivalence, it follows that so is \(\mathcal {A}\boxtimes F\). Conversely, assume that \(\mathcal {A}\boxtimes F\) is an equivalence, and choose a coalgebra C for \(\mathcal {A}\) as in 3.2.2.

For a given object X in \(\mathcal {A}\) (interpreted as a comodule), we have a commutative square

For \(A,B\in \mathcal {B}\), the equivalence \(\mathcal {A}\boxtimes F\) induces isomorphisms

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {End}_{C}(X)\otimes \operatorname {Hom}_{\mathcal {B}}(A,B)\xrightarrow {\sim }\operatorname {End}_C(X)\otimes \operatorname {Hom}_{\mathcal {B}'}(FA,FB), \end{aligned}$$

showing that F is fully faithful.

Now we consider the commutative square

where the downwards arrows are forgetful functors. For any object \(Y\in \mathcal {B}'\), there is some \(l\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\) such that \(Y^{\oplus l}\) is in the image of the downwards arrow, and hence in the image of F. Since F is fully faithful and \(\mathcal {B}'\) is Krull-Schmidt, it follows that also F is essentially surjective. \(\square \)

The following is a standard application of Lemma 3.1.2(2), which shows that one can refine the defining property of the Deligne product, from right exact functors to exact functors.

Lemma 3.2.9

For \(\mathcal {A},\mathcal {B},\mathcal {C}\) in \(\mathcal {T}ak\), restriction along \(\mathcal {A}\times \mathcal {B}\rightarrow \mathcal {A}\boxtimes \mathcal {B}\) yields an equivalence between the category of exact \(\Bbbk \)-linear functors \(\mathcal {A}\boxtimes \mathcal {B}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\) with the category of bilinear bifunctors \(\mathcal {A}\times \mathcal {B}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\) that are exact in each variable.

3.3 The Deligne product of tensor categories

In analogy with the notation \(\mathcal {T}ak^{ex}_{\Bbbk }\), we denote by \(\mathcal {T}ens_{\Bbbk }^{ex}\) the 2-category of tensor categories, tensor functors and natural transformations of monoidal functors and by \(\mathcal {T}ens_{\Bbbk }\) the 2-category of tensor categories, LSM functors and natural transformations of monoidal functors. We have obvious forgetful 2-functors to \(\mathcal {T}ak^{ex}_{\Bbbk }\) and \(\mathcal {T}ak_{\Bbbk }\), respectively. Note also that LSM functors between tensor categories are exact whenever they are right exact, by duality.

It is a classical fact from [12, §5] that \(-\boxtimes -\) from \(\mathcal {T}ak^{rex}\times \mathcal {T}ak^{rex}\) to \(\mathcal {T}ak^{rex}\) lifts to a pseudo-functor

$$\begin{aligned} -\boxtimes -:\;\mathcal {T}ens_{\Bbbk }^{ex}\times \mathcal {T}ens_{\Bbbk }^{ex}\;\rightarrow \; \mathcal {T}ens_{\Bbbk }^{ex}. \end{aligned}$$
(3.2)

We sketch a proof that allows us to generalise again to include non-exact functors.

3.3.1

Consider tensor categories \(\mathcal {C}_1,\mathcal {C}_2\) over \(\Bbbk \). The tensor structure on \(\mathcal {C}_i\) equips the coalgebra \(C_i\) (obtained from some choice of exact faithful \(\mathcal {C}_i\rightarrow \textrm{Vec}\)) with the structure of a copseudo-Hopf algebra, see [9, §2.5]. We can use this to equip \(\mathcal {C}_1\boxtimes \mathcal {C}_2\) with a unique structure of a tensor category for which the functors

$$\begin{aligned} -\boxtimes \textbf{1}:\mathcal {C}_1\rightarrow \mathcal {C}_1\boxtimes \mathcal {C}_2\quad \text{ and }\quad \textbf{1}\boxtimes -:\mathcal {C}_2\rightarrow \mathcal {C}_1\boxtimes \mathcal {C}_2\end{aligned}$$
(3.3)

are tensor functors, [12, Proposition 5.17]. Indeed, it follows quickly, see [12, §5.16], that there is a unique symmetric tensor product on \(\mathcal {C}_1\boxtimes \mathcal {C}_2\) compatible with \(\mathcal {C}_1\times \mathcal {C}_2\rightarrow \mathcal {C}_1\boxtimes \mathcal {C}_2\), the only subtlety is proving that the tensor product is exact. This is equivalent to \(\mathcal {C}_1\boxtimes \mathcal {C}_2\) being rigid, via Lemma 3.2.3(2), and only known to be true when \(\Bbbk \) is perfect, see the discussion in [11, §6]. The copseudo-Hopf algebra structure on \(C=C_1\) contains a \((C,C^{\otimes 2})\)-bicomodule T, see [9, Definition 2.1], so that the tensor product on \(\textrm{Comod}_C(\mathcal {C}_2)\) is given by

$$\begin{aligned} M\times N\;\mapsto \; T\Box ^{C\otimes C}(M\otimes N),\end{aligned}$$
(3.4)

where the occurrence of \(\otimes \) refers to the tensor product in \(\mathcal {C}_2\) of (the objects in \(\mathcal {C}_2\) underlying) M and N. The crucial observation is therefore Lemma 3.1.2(2) from which we can indeed derive exactness of the tensor product.

3.3.2

We can further show that the pseudo-functor in Equation (3.2) extends to a pseudo-functor

$$\begin{aligned} -\boxtimes -:\;\mathcal {T}ens_{\Bbbk }^{ex}\times \mathcal {T}ens_{\Bbbk }\;\rightarrow \; \mathcal {T}ens_{\Bbbk } \end{aligned}$$
(3.5)

which is compatible with the pseudo-functor in Proposition 3.2.6. Indeed, since T is injective as a right \({C\otimes C}\)-comodule, we have a canonical isomorphism of C-comodules

$$\begin{aligned} G\left( T\Box ^{C\otimes C}(M\otimes N)\right) \;\simeq \; T\Box ^{C\otimes C}(G(M\otimes N)), \end{aligned}$$

for all C-comodules M, N in \(\mathcal {C}_2\) and any \(\Bbbk \)-linear (not necessarily exact) functor \(G:\mathcal {C}_2\rightarrow \mathcal {C}_2'.\) Using this, one can show that the functor \(F\boxtimes G\), from Equation (3.2), for any (exact) tensor functor F and any LSM functor G is canonically LSM.

An instance of the coherence conditions of a pseudo-functor is the following example.

Example 3.3.3

Consider a tensor functor \(F:\mathcal {C}_1\rightarrow \mathcal {C}_2\) and an LSM functor \(\Theta :\mathcal {D}_1\rightarrow \mathcal {D}_2\), the following diagram of LSM functors is commutative

Lemma 3.3.4

Consider tensor categories \(\mathcal {C}_1,\mathcal {C}_2,\mathcal {C}\) over \(\Bbbk \). If

$$\begin{aligned} F:\mathcal {C}_1\boxtimes \mathcal {C}_2\;\rightarrow \;\mathcal {C}\end{aligned}$$

is an LSM functor that restricts under the functors in Equation (3.3) to tensor functors on \(\mathcal {C}_1,\mathcal {C}_2\), then F is exact, i.e. a tensor functor.

Proof

By Theorem 2.2.1 it is sufficient to show that F is faithful. Since every object in \(\mathcal {C}_1\boxtimes \mathcal {C}_2\) is a subobject and a quotient of an object \(X\boxtimes Y\), it suffices to prove that no non-zero morphism

$$\begin{aligned} X\boxtimes Y\;\rightarrow \;U\boxtimes V \end{aligned}$$

is sent to zero by F. However, the restriction of F to such objects corresponds to that of the (faithful) tensor functor \(\mathcal {C}_1\boxtimes \mathcal {C}_2\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\) given by the universal property of \(\mathcal {C}_1\boxtimes \mathcal {C}_2\) from the two restrictions of F. \(\square \)

3.3.5

For future use, we also record the following result. Consider a tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\) and \(\mathcal {A},\mathcal {B}\in \mathcal {T}ak\). Consider the functor

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {C}\times \mathcal {C}\times \mathcal {A}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\boxtimes \mathcal {A},\quad (X_1,X_2,A)\mapsto (X_1\otimes X_2)\boxtimes \mathcal {A}\end{aligned}$$

which is \(\Bbbk \)-linear and exact in each variable. We can reinterpret this as a functor

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {C}\times \mathcal {A}\;\rightarrow \;\operatorname {Fun}_{\Bbbk }(\mathcal {C},\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \mathcal {A}), \end{aligned}$$

leading via Lemma 3.2.9 to an exact functor with domain \(\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \mathcal {A}\). In turn we can interpret this as a functor

$$\begin{aligned} -\circledast -:\mathcal {C}\times (\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \mathcal {A})\;\rightarrow \;\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \mathcal {A}\end{aligned}$$

which is linear and exact in both variables. Such functors make \(\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \mathcal {A}\) and \(\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \mathcal {B}\) into module categories over \(\mathcal {C}\) in the sense of [16, §7.3].

Proposition 3.3.6

For a \(\Bbbk \)-linear functor \(\Theta :\mathcal {A}\rightarrow \mathcal {B}\), the \(\Bbbk \)-linear functor \(\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \Theta \) is a \(\mathcal {C}\)-module functor.

Proof

This follows from the commutative diagram

where \(\Delta :\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \mathcal {C}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\) is the exact functor corresponding to \(-\otimes -:\mathcal {C}\times \mathcal {C}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\) under Lemma 3.2.9. \(\square \)

3.4 The tensor power functor

Let \(\mathcal {C}\) be a tensor category and fix \(n\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\).

3.4.1

The category \(\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Rep}S_n\), see Example 3.2.4(1), is the tensor category of \(S_n\)-representations in \(\mathcal {C}\). The canonical example of an \(S_n\)-representation in \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(X^{\otimes n}\) equipped with the braiding action. It follows that

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {C}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Rep}S_n,\quad X\mapsto X^{\otimes n} \end{aligned}$$
(3.6)

is a well-defined symmetric monoidal (non-additive) functor.

Lemma 3.4.2

For every tensor functor \(F:\mathcal {C}\rightarrow \mathcal {D}\), the diagram of symmetric monoidal functors

is commutative.

Remark 3.4.3

Assume that \(\mathcal {C}\) has projective objects. Then we have the exact faithful functor

$$\begin{aligned} \omega =\bigoplus _P\operatorname {Hom}_{\mathcal {C}}(P,-):\;\mathcal {C}\rightarrow \textrm{Vec}, \end{aligned}$$

where P ranges over all projective covers of simple objects in \(\mathcal {C}\). We can then construct the following functor

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {C}\xrightarrow {(-)^{\otimes n}}\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Rep}S_n\xrightarrow {\omega \boxtimes \operatorname {Rep}S_n}\operatorname {Rep}S_n,\quad X\;\mapsto \;\bigoplus _P\operatorname {Hom}_{\mathcal {C}}(P, X^{\otimes n}), \end{aligned}$$

where we consider the obvious \(S_n\)-module structures.

4 \(\textbf{O}\)-functors

Let \(\Bbbk \) be an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(p>0\) and fix \(i\in \mathbb {Z}\).

4.1 Definitions

Let \(\mathcal {V}\) be a tensor category (over \(\Bbbk \)).

Definition 4.1.1

  1. (1)

    An \(\textbf{O}^i\{\mathcal {V}\}\)-functorFootnote 1\(\Phi \) is a family of \(\operatorname {Frob}^i\)-LSM functors

    $$\begin{aligned} \Phi _{\mathcal {C}}\;:\; \mathcal {C}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\boxtimes \mathcal {V}, \end{aligned}$$

    for every tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\) over \(\Bbbk \), such that, for each tensor functor \(F:\mathcal {C}\rightarrow \mathcal {D}\), the diagram of LSM functors

    is commutative up to a natural isomorphism (of monoidal functors).

  2. (2)

    Given an \(\textbf{O}^i\{\mathcal {V}\}\)-functor \(\Phi \), a tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\) is called \(\Phi \)-exact if \(\Phi _{\mathcal {C}}\) is exact, and hence a \(\operatorname {Frob}^i\)-tensor functor.

  3. (3)

    Given an \(\textbf{O}^i\{\mathcal {V}\}\)-functor \(\Phi \), the \(\Phi \)-type of \(\mathcal {C}\) is the minimal tensor subcategory \(\mathcal {V}_1\subset \mathcal {V}\) for which \(\Phi _{\mathcal {C}}\) takes values in

    $$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {C}\boxtimes \mathcal {V}_1\;\subset \; \mathcal {C}\boxtimes \mathcal {V}. \end{aligned}$$

Remark 4.1.2

One could make the definition of an \(\textbf{O}^i\{\mathcal {V}\}\)-functor stricter by adding the natural transformations for the commutative squares to the data and imposing coherence conditions. Concretely, we can consider the forgetful 2-functor from the 2-category of tensor categories and tensor functors to the 2-category of tensor categories and additive symmetric monoidal functors, and the composite of this 2-functor with the pseudo-functor \(-\boxtimes \mathcal {V}\). The stricter definition of an \(\textbf{O}^i\{\mathcal {V}\}\)-functor would be a pseudo-natural transformation (consisting of \(\operatorname {Frob}^i\)-linear functors) between these pseudo-functors. Since for the moment this additional structure does not seem to provide stronger results, we opted for the simplest functioning form of the definition. Nonetheless, \(\textbf{O}^i\{\mathcal {V}\}\)-functors constructed from \(\textbf{V}\)-functors as in the next section (and hence all \(\textbf{O}^i\{\mathcal {V}\}\)-functors considered in this paper) feature this extra structure.

Lemma 4.1.3

Consider a tensor functor \(F:\mathcal {C}'\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\) and an \(\textbf{O}^i\{\mathcal {V}\}\)-functor \(\Phi \).

  1. (1)

    If \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(\Phi \)-exact, then also \(\mathcal {C}'\) is \(\Phi \)-exact.

  2. (2)

    Let \(\mathcal {V}_1\) and \(\mathcal {V}_1'\) be the \(\Phi \)-types of \(\mathcal {C}\) and \(\mathcal {C}'\), then \(\mathcal {V}_1'\subset \mathcal {V}_1\).

Proof

Part (1) follows from commutativity of the diagram in Definition 4.1.1(1), and using either Theorem 2.2.1 or the fact that \(F\boxtimes \mathcal {V}\) is exact in Definition 4.1.1(1), by Equation (3.2).

Also part (2) follows from commutativity of the diagram in Definition 4.1.1(1), for instance by viewing \(\mathcal {C}'\) as a category of representations over some affine group scheme in \(\mathcal {C}\) as in [12, §7]. \(\square \)

4.1.4

Given a second tensor category \(\mathcal {V}'\) and an LSM-functor \(F:\mathcal {V}\rightarrow \mathcal {V}'\), using Lemma 3.3.3, we obtain an \(\textbf{O}^i\{\mathcal {V}'\}\)-functor from any \(\textbf{O}^i\{\mathcal {V}\}\)-functor \(\Phi \), by considering the composites

$$\begin{aligned} \Phi _{\mathcal {C}}':\;\mathcal {C}\xrightarrow {\Phi _{\mathcal {C}}}\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \mathcal {V}\xrightarrow {\mathcal {C}\boxtimes F}\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \mathcal {V}'. \end{aligned}$$

If F is exact (i.e. a tensor functor), we call the resulting \(\textbf{O}^i\{\mathcal {V}'\}\)-functor \(\Phi '\) a descendant of \(\Phi \).

If \(\Phi '\) is a descendant of \(\Phi \), then \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(\Phi \)-exact if and only if it is \(\Phi '\)-exact. Partly because of this, it is natural to focus on \(\textbf{O}^i\{\mathcal {V}\}\)-functors for incompressible \(\mathcal {V}\). In particular, we abbreviate \(\textbf{O}^i\{\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\}\) to \(\textbf{O}^i_n\) .

Example 4.1.5

  1. (1)

    The standard inclusion \(\mathcal {C}\simeq \mathcal {C}\boxtimes \textrm{Vec}\hookrightarrow \mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) is a trivial example of an \(\textbf{O}^0_n\)-functor.

  2. (2)

    The Frobenius functor

    $$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {Fr}:\mathcal {C}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_p \end{aligned}$$

    from [5, 17, 22] is an \(\textbf{O}^1_1\)-functor. Usually \(\operatorname {Fr}\)-exact categories are called Frobenius exact. The Frobenius functor \(\operatorname {Fr}\) is also a descendant of the enhanced Frobenius functor \(\operatorname {Fr}^{en}\), see [9, §3.2], which is an \(\textbf{O}^1\{\overline{\operatorname {Rep}S_p}\}\)-functor.

  3. (3)

    Assume that we are given an \(\textbf{O}^i\{\mathcal {V}\}\)-functor \(\Phi \). Consider the composite LSM functor

    $$\begin{aligned} H:\mathcal {V}\xrightarrow {\Sigma }\overline{\mathcal {V}}\rightarrow \operatorname {Ver}_p, \end{aligned}$$

    with the second functor the unique tensor functor to \(\operatorname {Ver}_p\), guaranteed to exist by the \(\operatorname {Ver}_p\)-Theorem (Theorem 2.3.4). Then the procedure in Sect. 4.1.4 yields the \(\textbf{O}^i_1\)-functor \(\overline{\Phi }\)

    $$\begin{aligned} \overline{\Phi }_{\mathcal {C}}: \; \mathcal {C}\xrightarrow {\Phi _{\mathcal {C}}}\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \mathcal {V}\xrightarrow {\mathcal {C}\boxtimes H}\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_p. \end{aligned}$$
    (4.1)

    Note that \(\overline{\Phi }\) is a descendant of \(\Phi \) if and only if \(\mathcal {V}\) is semisimple.

Lemma 4.1.6

Let \(\Phi \) be an \(\textbf{O}^i\{\mathcal {V}\}\)-functor, and \(\mathcal {C}\) and \(\mathcal {D}\) tensor categories.

  1. (1)

    If \(\mathcal {C}\) and \(\mathcal {D}\) are \(\Phi \)-exact, then so is \(\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \mathcal {D}\).

  2. (2)

    If \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(\overline{\Phi }\)-exact, then it is also \(\Phi \)-exact.

Proof

Part (1) is an example of Lemma 3.3.4. For part (2), it suffices (using Theorem 2.2.1) to observe that faithfulness of the composite Equation (4.1) implies in particular that \(\Phi _{\mathcal {C}}\) is faithful. \(\square \)

4.2 Potential properties

Our main motivation to introduce and study \(\textbf{O}\)-functors is their potential for replacing the Frobenius functor in the proof of the \(\operatorname {Ver}_p\)-Theorem towards proving the \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^\infty }\)-Conjecture. In this section, we therefore explore potential properties of \(\textbf{O}\)-functors that would be required to realise this. We fix \(n\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\) and an \(\textbf{O}^i_n\)-functor \(\Phi \).

4.2.1

We have the following potential properties of an \(\textbf{O}^i_n\)-functor \(\Phi \):

  1. (O0)

    \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) is \(\Phi \)-exact.

  2. (O1)

    We have \(\Phi _{\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}}(L_1)\simeq \textbf{1}\boxtimes L_1\) or (if \(p>2\)) \(\Phi _{\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}}(L_1)\simeq \bar{\textbf{1}}\boxtimes (\bar{\textbf{1}}\otimes L_1)\).

  3. (O2)

    A tensor category of moderate growth is \(\overline{\Phi }\)-exact if and only if it is \(\operatorname {Fr}\)-exact.

  4. (O3)

    Let \(\mathcal {C}_1\rightarrow \mathcal {C}_2\) be a surjective tensor functor, and assume that \(\mathcal {C}_1\) is \(\Phi \)-exact and of moderate growth. Then also \(\mathcal {C}_2\) is \(\Phi \)-exact.

As will be explained in the following subsection, the above technical properties are motivated by the below conceptual potential property, that \(\Phi \) determines which tensor categories ‘fibre’ over \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\):

  1. (OF)

    The following properties are equivalent on a tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\):

    1. (1)

      \(\mathcal {C}\) is of moderate growth and \(\Phi \)-exact;

    2. (2)

      \(\mathcal {C}\) admits a tensor functor to \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\).

Remark 4.2.2

  1. (1)

    The \(\operatorname {Ver}_p\)-Theorem states precisely that \(\operatorname {Fr}\) satisfies (OF) for \(n=1\).

  2. (2)

    By Corollary 2.3.7, (O1) implies (O0). Moreover, (O1) does not make sense for \(p^n=2\), so by convention for that case we redefine (O1) as (O0).

  3. (3)

    LSM functors are exact on semisimple tensor categories. It thus follows from the \(\operatorname {Ver}_p\)-Theorem that a Frobenius exact tensor category of moderate growth is \(\Psi \)-exact, for every \(\textbf{O}^i\{\mathcal {V}\}\)-functor \(\Psi \). In particular, the ‘if and only if’ condition in (O2) is always satisfied in one direction.

  4. (4)

    Condition (O3) is automatically satisfied when we only consider tensor categories with property (SP). Indeed, this follows from Lemma 2.2.2. That Condition (O3) is satisfied in general for the Frobenius functor was proved in [10].

4.3 Interpretation of the potential properties

In this section, we fix \(n\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\) and an \(\textbf{O}^i_n\)-functor \(\Phi \).

4.3.1

Summary In the quest for \(\textbf{O}\)-functors satisfying (OF), imposing Condition (O1) is natural. Indeed, by Corollary 2.3.7 it is one of only two options. It is the option that is satisfied by the Frobenius functor, and one of the indispensable properties exploited in [9] for proving the \(\operatorname {Ver}_p\)-Theorem. Once we accept (O1) and (OF), condition (O2) follows, by Theorem 4.3.2 below.

On the other hand, assumptions (O1) and (O2) are also sufficient to imply (OF). This is proved in Theorem 4.3.3 below, which contains the \(\operatorname {Ver}_p\)-Theorem as a special case, but is proved by reducing to that case.

The results in this section thus motivate the quest for \(\textbf{O}^i_n\)-functors satisfying (O1) and (O2). Moreover, Proposition 4.3.4 below motivates the quest for \(\textbf{O}^i_n\)-functors satisfying simply (O1); and Proposition 4.4.2 in the next section even motivates the quest for arbitrary \(\textbf{O}^i_n\)-functors.

Theorem 4.3.2

Assume that \(\Phi \) satisfies (OF), then:

  1. (1)

    \(\Phi \) satisfies (O0).

  2. (2)

    If \(\Phi \) satisfies (O1), then it also satisfies (O2).

  3. (3)

    Condition (O3) on \(\Phi \) is equivalent to the condition that \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) be Bezrukavnikov, as defined in [10].

Proof

Parts (1) and (3) follow by definition. Part (2) for \(n=1\) is a tautology by the \(\operatorname {Ver}_p\)-theorem, so we focus on \(n>1\). Consider a tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\) that is \(\overline{\Phi }\)-exact. Lemma 4.1.6(2) implies that \(\mathcal {C}\) is also \(\Phi \)-exact and so by assumption admits a tensor functor F to \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\). We have the commutative diagram

and by assumption (O1) on \(\Phi \) (and Corollary 2.3.7(1)), \(\overline{\Phi }_{\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}}\) takes values in the semisimple tensor category \(\textrm{sVec}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_p\). It follows that the upper path represents a \(\operatorname {Frob}^i\)-tensor functor from \(\mathcal {C}\) to a semisimple tensor category, so \(\mathcal {C}\) is indeed Frobenius exact. \(\square \)

Theorem 4.3.3

If \(\Phi \) satisfies (O1) and (O2), then the following are equivalent for a tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\) over \(\Bbbk \):

  1. (1)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(\Phi \)-exact and of moderate growth;

  2. (2)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) admits a tensor functor to \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\).

In other words, properties (O1) and (O2) together imply (OF).

Proof

That (2) implies (1) follows from assumption (O1). For convenience, we write out the proof that (1) implies (2) for \(p>2\) and for the option

$$\begin{aligned} \Phi (L_1)\;=\; \bar{\textbf{1}}\boxtimes (\bar{\textbf{1}}\otimes L_1) \end{aligned}$$

in (O1), the remaining case being identical up to notation.

Applying the commutative diagramFootnote 2 in Definition 4.1.1 to \(F=\Phi _{\mathcal {C}}\) shows that the two composites in

(4.2)

are isomorphic. By assumption (O1), the upper right functor takes values in

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {C}\boxtimes \textrm{sVec}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}. \end{aligned}$$

Indeed, this is true for objects \(X\boxtimes Y\) in \(\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) by Corollary 2.3.7(1), and hence true for all objects by exactness of \(\Phi _{\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}}\) in Lemma 4.1.6(1). Therefore both composites in Equation (4.2) also take values in this tensor subcategory.

The simple objects in \(\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) are of the form \(V_1\boxtimes V_2\), for simple objects \(V_1\in \mathcal {C}\), \(V_2\in \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\). Let \(V\in \mathcal {C}\) be any simple object for which there exists a simple \(V'\in \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\), for which \(V\boxtimes V'\) appears as a simple constituent (in the Jordan-Hölder series) of \(\Phi _{\mathcal {C}}(X)\) for some \(X\in \mathcal {C}\). Since \(\Phi _{\mathcal {C}}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) is exact, it thus follows from the previous paragraph that

$$\begin{aligned} \Phi _{\mathcal {C}}(V)\;\in \; \mathcal {C}\boxtimes \textrm{sVec}\;\subset \; \mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}. \end{aligned}$$

Let \(\mathcal {C}_1\) denote the Serre tensor subcategory of \(\mathcal {C}\) generated by all simple \(V\in \mathcal {C}\) as above. It then follows that \(\Phi _{\mathcal {C}}\) takes values in \(\mathcal {C}_1\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) and that \(\Phi _{\mathcal {C}_1}\) takes values in \(\mathcal {C}_1\boxtimes \textrm{sVec}\) (that is, the \(\Phi \)-type of \(\mathcal {C}_1\) is \(\textrm{Vec}\) or \(\textrm{sVec}\)).

Next we can observe that \(\mathcal {C}_1\) is \(\overline{\Phi }\)-exact. Indeed

$$\begin{aligned} \textrm{sVec}\hookrightarrow \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\rightarrow \overline{\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}}\rightarrow \operatorname {Ver}_p \end{aligned}$$

compose to the (exact) inclusion \(\textrm{sVec}\subset \operatorname {Ver}_p\). Consequently the composite \(\overline{\Phi }_{\mathcal {C}_1}\)

is indeed exact. By Assumption (O2) and the \(\operatorname {Ver}_p\)-Theorem, we therefore have a tensor functor \(F:\mathcal {C}_1\rightarrow \operatorname {Ver}_p\), yielding a \(\operatorname {Frob}^i\)-tensor functor

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {C}\xrightarrow {\Phi _{\mathcal {C}}}\mathcal {C}_1\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\xrightarrow {F\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}}\operatorname {Ver}_p\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\xrightarrow {\otimes }\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}. \end{aligned}$$

This concludes the proof, since by Remark 2.3.8, we can postcompose with a \(\operatorname {Frob}^{-i}\)-tensor functor \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\rightarrow \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\). \(\square \)

The following proposition is an example of the potential of \(\textbf{O}\)-functors in the structure theory of tensor categories. For the moment, we can only prove such a result for finite tensor categories.

Proposition 4.3.4

Assume that the \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^\infty }\)-Conjecture (see Conjecture 2.3.5) is true, and that \(p^n>2\). If \(\Phi \) satisfies (O1), then the following are equivalent on a finite tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\):

  1. (1)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(\Phi \)-exact;

  2. (2)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) admits a tensor functor to \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\).

As part of the proof of Proposition 4.3.4, we derive the following unconditional lemma.

Lemma 4.3.5

Assume that \(p^n>2\). Let \(\Phi \) be an \(\textbf{O}^i_n\)-functor satisfying (O1). Then \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^{n+1}}^+\) is not \(\Phi \)-exact.

Proof

Assume first that \(p>2\). Then \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^{n+1}}^+\) is generated by the simple object

$$\begin{aligned} L:=L_1^{[n+1]}\otimes \bar{\textbf{1}}= L_{1+p^{n}(p-2)}^{[n+1]}. \end{aligned}$$

Assume for a contradiction that \(\Phi _{\operatorname {Ver}_{p^{n+1}}^+}\) is exact. Since there is only one object with corresponding Frobenius–Perron dimension in the target, see [2, Corollary 4.44], we find that

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {Ver}_{p^{n+1}}^+\xrightarrow {\Phi }\operatorname {Ver}_{p^{n+1}}^+\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}, \quad L\mapsto L\boxtimes \textbf{1}. \end{aligned}$$

This implies that the functor is an equivalence onto the subcategory \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^{n+1}}^+\boxtimes \textrm{Vec}\). However, this contradicts assumption (O1) applied to \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\subset \operatorname {Ver}_{p^{n+1}}^+\).

Now consider \(p=2\) and hence \(n>1\). It follows from Assumption (O1) that, under

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {Ver}_{2^{n+1}}^+\;\xrightarrow {\Phi _{\operatorname {Ver}_{2^{n+1}}^+}}\;\operatorname {Ver}_{2^{n+1}}^+\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{2^n}, \end{aligned}$$

the generator \(L_1\) of \(\operatorname {Ver}_{2^n}\subset \operatorname {Ver}_{2^{n+1}}^+\) is sent to \(\textbf{1}\boxtimes L_1\).

On the other hand, \(\operatorname {Ver}_{2^{n+1}}^+\) is incompressible, so the displayed functor is an equivalence onto a tensor subcategory of the right-hand side. We also observe that \(\operatorname {Ver}_{2^{n+1}}^+\) is indecomposable as an additive category, see [1, Theorem 2.1(viii)], whereas the right-hand side decomposes into the tensor subcategory \(\operatorname {Ver}_{2^{n+1}}^+\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{2^n}^+\) and a subcategory equivalent to \(\operatorname {Ver}_{2^{n+1}}^+\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{2^{n-1}}\), see [1, Theorem 2.1(ix)]. Hence, we find that the displayed functor takes values in \(\operatorname {Ver}_{2^{n+1}}^+\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{2^n}^+\), which contradicts the conclusion from the previous paragraph. \(\square \)

Lemma 4.3.6

Assume that the \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^\infty }\)-Conjecture is true and that \({\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}}\) is \(\Phi \)-exact (i.e. \(\Phi \) satisfies (O0)), but \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^{n+1}}^+\) is not \(\Phi \)-exact. Then a finite tensor category is \(\Phi \)-exact if and only if it admits a tensor functor to \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\).

Proof

This follows from Corollary 2.2.3 and the classification of tensor subcategories of \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) in [2, Corollary 4.61]. \(\square \)

Proof of Proposition 4.3.4

The conclusion follows immediately from the combination of Lemma 4.3.5 and Lemma 4.3.6. \(\square \)

4.4 \(\textbf{O}\)-functors and incompressible categories

Here we show that to any \(\textbf{O}\)-functor \(\Phi \) (without further assumptions), we can associate an incompressible category so that \(\Phi \) controls which tensor categories fibre over it.

4.4.1

By a class of incompressible categories, we mean a family \(\{\mathcal {C}_\alpha \}\) of incompressible categories for which \(\mathcal {C}_\alpha \), for every \(\alpha \), is equivalent to a tensor subcategory of \(\mathcal {C}_\beta \) for every \(\beta \).

The \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^\infty }\)-Conjecture predicts in particular that classes of incompressible categories of moderate growth are simply equivalence classes.

Proposition 4.4.2

Let \(\mathcal {V}\) be a tensor category and \(\Phi \) an \(\textbf{O}^i\{\mathcal {V}\}\)-functor. There exists a unique class of incompressible categories \(\{\mathcal {C}_\alpha \}\), all satisfying (SP), for which the following properties are equivalent on every finite tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\):

  1. (1)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(\Phi \)-exact;

  2. (2)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) admits a tensor functor to some \(\mathcal {C}_\alpha \);

  3. (3)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) admits a tensor functor to every \(\mathcal {C}_\alpha \).

Proof

Consider the collection of all finite incompressible tensor categories which are \(\Phi \)-exact. It is non-empty as it contains \(\textrm{Vec}\). By [10, Corollary 5.2.8], there exists an incompressible tensor category \(\mathcal {D}\) which contains all these finite incompressible categories as tensor subcategories. If necessary, we replace \(\mathcal {D}\) by its minimal tensor subcategory which contains all these finite subcategories. By construction \(\mathcal {D}\) satisfies (SP) and is \(\Phi \)-exact.

Now let \(\mathcal {C}\) be an arbitrary \(\Phi \)-exact finite tensor category. By [10, Theorem 5.2.1], \(\mathcal {C}\) admits a surjective tensor functor to an incompressible tensor category. By surjectivity, this tensor category is finite. By Remark 4.2.2(3), this finite tensor category is also \(\Phi \)-exact. By the previous paragraph, \(\mathcal {C}\) thus admits a tensor functor to \(\mathcal {D}\). In conclusion a finite tensor category is \(\Phi \)-exact if and only if it admits a tensor functor to \(\mathcal {D}\).

Now we let \(\{\mathcal {C}_\alpha \}\) be the unique class of incompressible categories that \(\mathcal {D}\) belongs to. This is the collection of those incompressible tensor subcategories of \(\mathcal {D}\) which themselves also contain a tensor subcategory equivalent to \(\mathcal {D}\). The statement of the proposition now follows. \(\square \)

Remark 4.4.3

If we assume that \(\Phi \) satisfies (O3), or strictly speaking its immediate generalisation from \(\textbf{O}^i_n\)-functors to \(\textbf{O}^i\{\mathcal {V}\}\)-functors, we can write a version of Proposition 4.4.2 without finiteness assumptions, with identical proof.

5 Construction of \(\textbf{O}\)-functors

Let p be a prime and \(\Bbbk \) an algebraically closed field of characteristic p.

5.1 \(\textbf{V}\)-functors

Let \(G<\textrm{Perm}(W)\) be a permutation group, for a finite set W.

Definition 5.1.1

A \(\textbf{V}\)-functor for \(G<\textrm{Perm}(W)\) is an LSM functor

$$\begin{aligned} \Theta :\operatorname {Rep}_{\Bbbk }G\;\rightarrow \; \mathcal {V}\end{aligned}$$

to a tensor category \(\mathcal {V}\) over \(\Bbbk \) with the condition that for every non-transitive subgroup \(H<G\),

$$\begin{aligned} \Theta (\operatorname {Ind}^G_{H}\textbf{1})=0. \end{aligned}$$

Given any tensor functor \(F:\mathcal {V}\rightarrow \mathcal {V}'\) and \(\textbf{V}\)-functor \(\Theta :\operatorname {Rep}G\rightarrow \mathcal {V}\), we obtain a \(\textbf{V}\)-functor \(F\circ \Theta \), which we call a descendant of \(\Theta \).

Remark 5.1.2

A G-module is called H-projective if it appears as a direct summand of a G-module which is induced from H. It follows that an LSM functor to a tensor category is a \(\textbf{V}\)-functor if and only if it annihilates all H-projective modules for all non-transitive \(H<G\).

Lemma 5.1.3

The following conditions are equivalent on \(G<\textrm{Perm}(W)\).

  1. (1)

    There exist \(\textbf{V}\)-functors for G;

  2. (2)

    The semisimplification \(\Sigma :\operatorname {Rep}G\rightarrow \overline{\operatorname {Rep}G}\) is a \(\textbf{V}\)-functor;

  3. (3)

    There is a p-subgroup \(P<G\) of G that acts transitively on W;

  4. (4)

    |W| is a power of p and G acts transitively on W.

Proof

First we prove that (1) implies (3). Let \(P<G\) be a Sylow p-subgroup. Then \(\operatorname {Ind}^G_P\textbf{1}\) has categorical dimension different from zero, and cannot be sent to zero under an LSM functor. Under assumption (1) it thus follows that P acts transitively on W, implying (3).

Obviously, (2) implies (1).

We prove that (3) implies (2). It follows from (3) and Sylow’s theorems that p divides |G : H| for every non-transitive subgroup \(H<G\).
