By for instance [18, §2 and §4], the module \(\operatorname {Ind}^G_{H}\textbf{1}\) is zero in the semisimplification (negligible) if and only if p divides |G : H|, which thus implies (2).

Clearly (3) implies (4). That (4) implies (3) follows from the standard fact that if a finite group G acts transitively on a set W of cardinality \(p^n\), then so does any p-Sylow subgroup. For completeness we include the proof:

Pick \(x\in W\). Then the stabiliser subgroup \(G_x<G\) satisfies

$$\begin{aligned} |G|=|G_x||W|=rp^{m+n} \end{aligned}$$

for some \(m\ge 0\) and r not divisible by p. Now for a p-Sylow subgroup \(P<G\) we have

$$\begin{aligned} p^{m+n}=|P|=|P_x||P\cdot x|, \end{aligned}$$

where \(|P_x|\) divides \(p^m\) (since \(P_x<G_x\)) and \(|P\cdot x|\le p^n\). Hence \(|P_x|=p^m\) and \(|P\cdot x|= p^n\), meaning \(P\cdot x=W\). \(\square \)

Remark 5.1.4

Due to Lemma 5.1.3, it is logical to focus on minimal transitive p-groups. Even though in the sequel we will focus on one particular family, this is still a very rich class of permutation groups. Examples include \(C_p<S_p\) or, more generally, \(C_{p^{n_1}}\times \dots \times C_{p^{n_t}}<S_{p^{n_1+\dots +n_t}}\), see Sect. 5.1.5 for the case \(n_i=1\). There are also semidirect product groups \(C_8\rtimes C_2\) or \(C_2^3\rtimes C_4\) which are minimal transitive subgroups of \(S_{16}\).

5.1.5

For the remainder of the section, we fix \(n\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\) and set

$$\begin{aligned} W\;:=\;\{1,2,\cdots ,p^n\}. \end{aligned}$$

For every \(a\in W\) we consider the p-adic expansion

$$\begin{aligned} a-1\;=\;\sum _{i=1}^n a_i p^{i-1} \end{aligned}$$

with \(0\le a_i<p\). For each \(1\le i\le n\), we then have a subgroup \(C_p<S_{p^n}\) generated by the permutation which sends \(1\le a\le p^n\) to \(a'\), so that the p-adic expansions of \(a-1\) and \(a'-1\) are identical, except that \(a_i\) is replaced by \(a_i+1\) modulo p.

We will henceforth focus our attention on the resulting class of transitive permutation p-groups

$$\begin{aligned} C_p^n=\prod _{i=1}^nC_p \;<\; S_{p^n}. \end{aligned}$$

Example 5.1.6

  1. (1)

    For \(G=C_p^2<S_{p^2}\), all \(p+1\) non-trivial proper subgroups \(H<G\) (i.e. those subgroups isomorphic to \(C_p\)) are non-transitive. The corresponding modules \(\operatorname {Ind}^G_{H}\textbf{1}\) have homological support labelled by the \(p+1\) points of \(\mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_p)\subset \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\).

  2. (2)

    In case \(p=2\) and \(n=2\), the permutation group \(C_2^{2}<S_4\) consists of the identity and the permutations

    $$\begin{aligned} (12)(34),\; (13)(24)\;\text{ and }\; (14)(23). \end{aligned}$$

Remark 5.1.7

A more intrinsic definition of the permutation group in Sect. 5.1.5 is as follows. If we let \(C_p^n\) act on itself via (left or right) multiplication, then the corresponding permutation group

$$\begin{aligned} C_p^{n}\;<\;\textrm{Perm}(C_p^n) \end{aligned}$$

gives our set-up (after a suitable enumeration of the elements in \(C_p^n\)).

5.1.8

Sect. 6 will be devoted to classifying all \(\textbf{V}\)-functors for the permutation group \(C_2^2<S_4\) from Example 5.1.6(2), while Sect. 5.3 – Sect. 5.4 work towards a specific case for the more general \(C_p^n<S_{p^n}\). Here we point out the lack of ‘interesting’ \(\textbf{V}\)-functors for another class of minimal transitive p-groups, namely \(C_{p^n}<S_{p^n}\). In particular, for \(S_4\), this leaves only \(C_2^2<S_4\) as interesting minimal 2-subgroup.

Lemma 5.1.9

The only \(\textbf{V}\)-functors for the permutation group \(C_{p^n}<S_{p^n}\) are the descendants of the semisimplification \(\Sigma :\operatorname {Rep}C_{p^n}\rightarrow \overline{\operatorname {Rep}C_{p^n}}\).

Proof

The classification of indecomposable modules in \(\operatorname {Rep}C_{p^n}\) comprises one isomorphism class \(M_i\) for every dimension \(1\le i\le p^n\). If \(\Theta \) is a \(\textbf{V}\)-functor then, by Remark 5.1.2, it sends every \(M_{ap}=\operatorname {Ind}^{C_{p^n}}_{C_{p^{n-1}}}M_a\), for \(1\le a\le p^{n-1}\) to zero (where we abuse notation by labelling indecomposable modules \(C_{p^{n-1}}\) again by \(M_{a}\)). In other words, \(\Theta (M_i)=0\) if and only if p divides \(i=\dim M_i\) if and only if \(\Sigma (M_i)=0\).

Now, set \(X:=\Theta (M_2)\), which is an object in a tensor category \(\mathcal {V}\). By construction there appear only finitely many indecomposable summands in the tensor powers \(X^{\otimes m}\). It then follows from the previous paragraph that the growth dimension of X, as defined for instance in [9, §4], must be the same as that of \(\Sigma (M_2)\). By construction the latter is strictly smaller than \(2=\dim M_2\). Hence X is simple, and therefore \(\Theta \) must send \(\textbf{1}\hookrightarrow M_2\) to zero. Indeed, by duality, the alternative implies that there exist \(\textbf{1}\hookrightarrow X\) and \(X\twoheadrightarrow \textbf{1}\) in \(\mathcal {V}\) which compose to zero.

But if \(\textbf{1}\hookrightarrow M_2\) is sent to zero by \(\Theta \), then its kernel includes all morphisms \(\textbf{1}\rightarrow M_i\) for \(i>1\), meaning it must be the ideal of negligible morphisms. \(\square \)

5.2 \(\textbf{O}\)-functors from \(\textbf{V}\)-functors

Recall the symmetric monoidal functor in Equation (3.6) and fix \(i\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\).

Theorem 5.2.1

Given a permutation group \(G<S_{p^i}\) and a \(\textbf{V}\)-functor \(\Theta : \operatorname {Rep}G\rightarrow \mathcal {V}\), the family of \(\operatorname {Frob}^i\)-LSM functors

$$\begin{aligned} \Phi _{\mathcal {C}}:\;\mathcal {C}\xrightarrow {X\mapsto X^{\otimes p^i}}\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Rep}S_{p^i}\xrightarrow {\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Res}}\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Rep}G\xrightarrow {\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \Theta }\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \mathcal {V}\end{aligned}$$

yields an \(\textbf{O}^i\{\mathcal {V}\}\)-functor.

Proof

For \(n=p^i\), the composite LSM functor

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {Rep}S_n\xrightarrow {\operatorname {Res}^{S_n}_G}\operatorname {Rep}G\xrightarrow {\Theta }\mathcal {V}\end{aligned}$$

sends \(\operatorname {Ind}^{S_n}_{S_\lambda }M\) to zero, for every \(\lambda \vdash n\), other than \(\lambda =(n)\), and \(M\in \operatorname {Rep}_{\Bbbk } S_{\lambda }\). Indeed, we can reduce this to the case \(M=\Bbbk \), which in turn follows from Mackey’s theorem.

By definition, \(\Phi _{\mathcal {C}}\) is symmetric monoidal. Since

$$\begin{aligned} (X\oplus Y)^{\otimes p^i}\;\simeq \; X^{\otimes p^i}\oplus Y^{\otimes p^i}\oplus \bigoplus _{j=1}^{p^i-1} \operatorname {Ind}^{S_{p^i}}_{S_{p^i-j}\times S_j}(X^{\otimes p^i-j}\otimes Y^{\otimes j}), \end{aligned}$$

it follows from the previous paragraph that \(\Phi _{\mathcal {C}}\) is additive. Since all but the first functor in the composition of \(\Phi _{\mathcal {C}}\) are \(\Bbbk \)-linear, it follows that \(\Phi _{\mathcal {C}}(\lambda f)=\lambda ^{p^j}\Phi _{\mathcal {C}}(f)\), for a morphism f and \(\lambda \in \Bbbk \), so \(\Phi _{\mathcal {C}}\) is \(\operatorname {Frob}^i\)-linear.

That the diagrams in Definition 4.1.1(1) are commutative follows from Lemma 3.4.2 and Lemma 3.3.3. \(\square \)

We have an obvious compatibility between the notions of descendants of \(\textbf{V}\)-functors and of \(\textbf{O}^i\)-functors, via Theorem 5.2.1.

Example 5.2.2

The Frobenius functor \(\operatorname {Fr}\) is obtained by the principle in Theorem 5.2.1 applied to the permutation group \(C_p<S_p\) and the \(\textbf{V}\)-functor

$$\begin{aligned} \Sigma :\operatorname {Rep}C_p\rightarrow \overline{\operatorname {Rep}C_p}. \end{aligned}$$

Proposition 5.2.3

Consider a permutation group \(G<S_{p^i}\) and two \(\textbf{V}\)-functors \(\Theta ^j:\operatorname {Rep}G\rightarrow \mathcal {V}_j\) with kernels \(J_j\), for \(j\in \{1,2\}\). Denote by \(\Phi ^1\), \(\Phi ^2\) the resulting \(\textbf{O}^i\{\mathcal {V}_j\}\)-functors from Theorem 5.2.1. Let \(\mathcal {C}\) be a \(\Phi ^2\)-exact tensor category.

  1. (1)

    If \(J_1\subset J_2\), then \(\mathcal {C}\) is also \(\Phi ^1\)-exact.

  2. (2)

    Assume that \(\mathcal {C}\) has property (P). If every object (whose identity morphism is) in \(J_1\) is also in \(J_2\), then \(\mathcal {C}\) is also \(\Phi ^1\)-exact.

Proof

Fix a faithful exact functor \(\omega :\mathcal {C}\rightarrow \textrm{Vec}\), leading to commutative diagrams

where the top row composes to \(\Phi _{\mathcal {C}}^j\) and the bottom row composes to \(\Theta ^j\).

By Theorem 2.2.1, \(\Phi ^j\)-exactness is determined by faithfulness of the top row. Since the two arrows to \(\mathcal {V}_j\) are faithful, \(\Phi ^j\)-exactness is thus determined by faithfulness of the composite functor

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {C}\rightarrow \operatorname {Rep}G\rightarrow (\operatorname {Rep}G)/J_j, \end{aligned}$$

where the first functor does not depend on j. Part (1) follows immediately and part (2) follows by adding in Lemma 2.2.2. \(\square \)

Proposition 5.2.4

Consider a \(\textbf{V}\)-functor \(\Theta :\operatorname {Rep}G\rightarrow \mathcal {V}\) for a permutation group \(G<S_{p^i}\) and the resulting \(\textbf{O}^i\{\mathcal {V}\}\)-functor \(\Phi \). Let \(\mathcal {C}\) be a tensor category with (enough) projective objects. Then the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(\Phi \)-exact;

  2. (2)

    there are projective objects P, Q in \(\mathcal {C}\) with \(\Theta (\operatorname {Hom}(Q,P^{\otimes p^i}))\not =0\);

  3. (3)

    for each projective object P in \(\mathcal {C}\), there is a projective object Q for which \(\Theta (\operatorname {Hom}(Q,P^{\otimes p^i}))\not =0\).

Proof

This is an immediate application of Lemma 2.2.2 and Remark 3.4.3. \(\square \)

Example 5.2.5

A tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\) with projective objects is Frobenius exact if and only if there are projective objects P, Q in \(\mathcal {C}\) for which the \(S_p\)-representation \(\operatorname {Hom}(Q,P^{\otimes p})\) has a non-negligible (meaning non-projective) summand.

Remark 5.2.6

Consider the functor

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {C}\xrightarrow {(-)^{\otimes p^i}}\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Rep}S_{p^i}\xrightarrow {\omega \boxtimes \operatorname {Rep}S_{p^i}}\operatorname {Rep}S_{p^i}, \end{aligned}$$

for a faithful exact functor \(\omega :\mathcal {C}\rightarrow \textrm{Vec}\). For the moment it is an open question how surjective this functor is in general, see [8] for some recent results. If there exists a suitable monoidal subcategory \(\mathcal {R}\subset \operatorname {Rep}S_{p^i}\) in which this functor has to take values for all \(\mathcal {C}\) (of moderate growth), one could introduce partially defined \(\textbf{V}\)-functors \(\mathcal {R}\rightarrow \mathcal {V}\), which would still lead to \(\textbf{O}\)-functors.

5.3 Interlude: tilting modules

We denote the affine group scheme (over \(\mathbb {Z}\)) of 2 by 2 matrices with determinant 1 by \(SL_2\). So for any field K, we have the corresponding abstract group \(SL_2(K)\). We also consider subgroups

$$\begin{aligned} U,T<B<SL_2, \end{aligned}$$

where B contains those matrices with entry 0 above the diagonal, and U additionally with entry 1 on the diagonal, and T consists of diagonal matrices.

We fix \(n\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\). When considering the elementary abelian p-group \(C_p^n\), we denote the generators by

$$\begin{aligned} g_i=(0,0,\cdots , 1, 0,\cdots 0)\in C_p\times C_p\times \cdots \times C_p, \end{aligned}$$

with the generator 1 of \(C_p=\mathbb {Z}/(p)\) in position i.

5.3.1

We consider elements (with \(\Bbbk ^+\) the additive group of the field)

$$\begin{aligned} {\underline{\lambda }}=(\lambda _1,\lambda _2,\cdots , \lambda _n)\,\in \,\mathbb {A}^{n}(\Bbbk )\;\xrightarrow {1:1}\; \operatorname {Hom}(C_p^n,\Bbbk ^+), \end{aligned}$$

where the bijection sends \({\underline{\lambda }}\) to the group homomorphism \(\{g_i\mapsto \lambda _i\}\).

We denote the subset of \(\mathbb {A}^n(\Bbbk )\) of elements that correspond to injective group homomorphisms by

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbb {A}^n_f(\Bbbk )\;\subset \;\mathbb {A}^n(\Bbbk ). \end{aligned}$$

One can describe this subset explicitly as the set of \(\mathbb {F}_p\)-linearly independent tuples, but we do not require this presently.

For the rest of this section, we fix \({\underline{\lambda }}\in \mathbb {A}^n_f(\Bbbk )\). We denote by

$$\begin{aligned} U_n<\Bbbk ^+=U(\Bbbk )<SL_2(\Bbbk ) \end{aligned}$$

the image of the corresponding group homomorphism \(C_p^n\hookrightarrow \Bbbk ^+\).

Example 5.3.2

The most canonical choice is \(U_n=U(\mathbb {F}_{p^n})\), which corresponds to choosing \({\underline{\lambda }}\) such that \(\{\lambda _i\}\subset \Bbbk \) form a basis of \(\mathbb {F}_{p^n}\) over \(\mathbb {F}_p\).

5.3.3

Recall from Example 2.1.3 that \(\operatorname {Rep}_{\Bbbk } SL_2\) is the category of finite-dimensional rational \(SL_2(\Bbbk )\)-representations, and recall from Sect. 2.3.1 the basic properties of \(\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2\subset \operatorname {Rep}SL_2\). We will focus on the forgetful (restriction) functor

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {Rep}_{\Bbbk } SL_2\;\subset \; \operatorname {Rep}_{\Bbbk } SL_2(\Bbbk )\;\rightarrow \;\operatorname {Rep}_{\Bbbk }U(\Bbbk )\;\rightarrow \operatorname {Rep}_{\Bbbk }U_n \end{aligned}$$
(5.1)

and more precisely on the composite functor

$$\begin{aligned} R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\;:\; \operatorname {Tilt}SL_2\hookrightarrow \operatorname {Rep}_{\Bbbk } SL_2\rightarrow \operatorname {Rep}_{\Bbbk } U_n\xrightarrow {\sim } \operatorname {Rep}_{\Bbbk }C_p^n \end{aligned}$$
(5.2)

We will use the same symbol for an \(SL_2\)-representation and for its restriction to \(U_n\). For V the natural \(SL_2(\Bbbk )\)-representation, we set

$$\begin{aligned} V_{{\underline{\lambda }}}:= R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(V)\;\in \;\operatorname {Rep}_{\Bbbk }C_p^n. \end{aligned}$$

We denote by

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {D}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\;\subset \; \operatorname {Rep}C_p^n, \end{aligned}$$

the essential image of \(R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\), which is the full monoidal subcategory of \(\operatorname {Rep}_{\Bbbk }C_p^n\) comprising direct summands of direct sums of tensor powers of \(V_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\). We denote by \(\mathcal {K}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\) the tensor ideal of \(\mathcal {D}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\) generated by any monomorphism \(\textbf{1}\hookrightarrow V_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\) (which is unique up to a scalar).

Remark 5.3.4

The representation \(V_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\) depends, up to isomorphism, only on the image of \({\underline{\lambda }}\) in \(\mathbb {P}^{n-1}(\Bbbk )\). Moreover, \(\mathbb {P}^{n-1}(\Bbbk )\) canonically parametrises indecomposable two-dimensional \(C_p^n\)-representations, while the image of \(\mathbb {A}^n_f(\Bbbk )\rightarrow \mathbb {P}^{n-1}(\Bbbk )\) parametrises faithful two-dimensional representations.

Recall from Sect. 2.3.1 that \(I_n\) is defined as the tensor ideal generated by the n-th Steinberg module \(St_n=T_{p^n-1}\) in \(\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2\).

Theorem 5.3.5

  1. (1)

    There is a faithful LSM functor \((\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2)/I_n\rightarrow \operatorname {Stab}C_p^n\) that fits into the commutative diagram

  2. (2)

    There is an LSM-equivalence \((\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2)/I_n\rightarrow \mathcal {D}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}/\mathcal {K}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\) that fits into the commutative diagram

By slight abuse of notation, we will denote both functors constructed in Theorem 5.3.5 again by \(R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\). The remainder of this subsection is devoted to the proof of Theorem 5.3.5. We denote by \(\nabla _i\), \(i\in \mathbb {N}\), the Weyl modules of \(SL_2\), see [20].

Lemma 5.3.6

For all \(0\le i<p^n\), we have

  1. (1)

    \(\dim _{\Bbbk }\operatorname {Hom}_{U_n}(\textbf{1},\nabla _i)=1\),

  2. (2)

    \(\dim _{\Bbbk }\operatorname {Hom}_{U_n}(V,\nabla _i)={\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1& \text{ if } \,i=0, \\ 2& \text{ if } \,i>0.\end{array}\right. }\)

Proof

We can realise \(\nabla _i\) as the degree i component of the graded algebra \(\Bbbk [x,y]\), with x, y in degree 1. The action of \(\lambda \in \Bbbk \simeq U(\Bbbk )\) is then given by

$$\begin{aligned} x^{a}y^b\;\mapsto \; (x+\lambda y)^ay^b. \end{aligned}$$

The condition on a vector \(\sum _jc_jx^{i-j}y^j\) in \(\nabla _i\) to be \(U_n\)-invariant is thus expressed in terms of polynomials over \(\Bbbk \) of degree bounded by \(i<p^n=|U_n|\) being zero when evaluated at every \(\lambda \in U_n\subset \Bbbk \). Hence all coefficients must be identically zero, yielding

$$\begin{aligned} \left( {\begin{array}{c}i-j\\ l\end{array}}\right) c_j=0,\quad \text{ for } \text{ all } \;1\le l\le i-j.\end{aligned}$$
(5.3)

Picking \(l=i-j\) shows that \(c_j=0\) for all \(j<i\), leaving indeed only a one-dimensional space of invariants, proving part (1).

The condition for a vector to be in the image of the generator of V is the same as the ones in Equation (5.3), but omitting the case \( j=i-1\). This proves part (2). \(\square \)

Remark 5.3.7

The bound \(i<p^n\) in Lemma 5.3.6 is sharp. Indeed, taking \(U_n:=U(\mathbb {F}_{p^n})\) allows one to compute directly that parts (1) and (2) fail for \(i=p^n\).

For a rational \(SL_2\)-representation M with a \(\nabla \)-flag (good filtration in the terminology of [20]), we denote the length of this filtration by \(\ell ^{\nabla }(M)\). For example, \(\ell ^\nabla (\nabla _i)=1\).

Proposition 5.3.8

For all \(0\le i<p^n\), we have

  1. (1)

    \(\dim _{\Bbbk }\operatorname {Hom}_{U_n}(\textbf{1},T_i)\,=\,\ell ^\nabla (T_i),\)

  2. (2)

    \(\dim _{\Bbbk }\operatorname {Hom}_{U_n}(V,T_i)\,=\,2\ell ^\nabla (T_i)-\dim _{\Bbbk }\operatorname {Hom}_{SL_2}(\textbf{1},T_{i})\).

Proof

We start with part (1). By Lemma 5.3.6(1), we already know that

$$\begin{aligned} \dim _{\Bbbk }\operatorname {Hom}_{U_n}(\textbf{1},T_i)\,\le \,\ell ^\nabla (T_i). \end{aligned}$$

To prove the inequality in the other direction, we will prove the stronger claim

$$\begin{aligned} \dim _{\Bbbk }\operatorname {Hom}_{U}(\textbf{1},T_i)\,\ge \,\ell ^\nabla (T_i), \end{aligned}$$

where the left-hand side now takes into account the action of the affine group scheme U. We can equivalently prove

$$\begin{aligned} \sum _{j\in \mathbb {N}}\dim _{\Bbbk }\operatorname {Hom}_{B}(\textbf{1}_{-j},T_i)\,\ge \,\ell ^\nabla (T_i), \end{aligned}$$

where \(\textbf{1}_{-j}\) stands for the 1-dimensional rational B-representation on which \(x\in \Bbbk ^\times = T(\Bbbk )\) acts via \( x^{-j}\). The latter now follows from weight considerations. Indeed, if the lowest weight appearing in \(M\in \operatorname {Rep}_{\Bbbk }B\) is \(-j\), then

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {Hom}_{B}(\textbf{1}_{-j}, M)\;=\;\operatorname {Hom}_T(\textbf{1}_{-j},M). \end{aligned}$$

Furthermore, \(T_i\) has a filtration (over \(SL_2\))

$$\begin{aligned} 0=M_{-1}\subset M_{0}\subset M_1\subset \cdots \subset M_i=T_i, \end{aligned}$$

where \(M_a/M_{a-1}\) is a direct sum of copies of \(\nabla _a\). Hence, the left-hand side of

$$\begin{aligned} \dim \operatorname {Hom}_B(\textbf{1}_{-j},M_j)\;\le \;\dim \operatorname {Hom}_B(\textbf{1}_{-j},T_i) \end{aligned}$$

equals the number of appearances of \(\nabla _{j}\) in the \(\nabla \)-flag of \(T_i\), proving part (1).

Now we consider part (2). We have

$$\begin{aligned} \dim \operatorname {Hom}_{SL_2}(\textbf{1}, T_i)\;=\;\dim M_0. \end{aligned}$$

By Lemma 5.3.6(2), we thus find

$$\begin{aligned} \dim _{\Bbbk }\operatorname {Hom}_{U_n}(V,T_i)\,\le \,2\ell ^\nabla (T_i)-\dim _{\Bbbk }\operatorname {Hom}_{SL_2}(\textbf{1},T_{i}). \end{aligned}$$

We can then conclude the proof similarly to part (1), by considering various lifts of V to B. \(\square \)

Proof of Theorem 5.3.5

Denote by \(\mathcal {D}\subset \operatorname {Rep}U_n\) the essential image of the category of \(SL_2\)-tilting modules under the functor in Equation (5.1). In other words, \(\mathcal {D}\) is simply \(\mathcal {D}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\) under the isomorphism \(U_n\simeq C_p^n\). We denote by \(\mathcal {K}\) the ideal in \(\mathcal {D}\) corresponding to \(\mathcal {K}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\) in \(\mathcal {D}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\) and write \(\mathcal {E}=\mathcal {D}/\mathcal {K}\). We will prove the statements in the theorem in their equivalent guise in terms of \(U_n\) and Equation (5.1), rather than \(C_p^n\) and Equation (5.2).

The functor in Eq. 5.1 sends the generator \(St_n\) of \(I_n\) to \(\Bbbk U_n\). Indeed, since \(St_n\) is \(\nabla _{p^n-1}\), it follows from Proposition 5.3.8(1) that

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {Hom}_{U_n}(\textbf{1}, St_{n})\;\simeq \;\Bbbk , \end{aligned}$$

so the conclusion follows from \(\dim _{\Bbbk } St_n=p^n\). It follows that Eq. 5.1 yields a faithful functor

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {Tilt}SL_2/I_n\;\hookrightarrow \;\operatorname {Stab}U_n, \end{aligned}$$

already proving part (1). The ideal \(\mathcal {K}\), being non-zero, contains all morphisms through projective \(U_n\)-modules, so we arrive indeed at an LSM functor

$$\begin{aligned} (\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2)/I_n\;\rightarrow \; \mathcal {E}. \end{aligned}$$
(5.4)

admitting the commutative diagram of part (2). It remains to prove this functor is an equivalence.

By construction, the functor in Equation (5.4) is essentially surjective. Since it is also additive monoidal, and the categories are rigid, it suffices to prove that

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {Hom}_{SL_2}(\textbf{1}, T_i)\;\rightarrow \; \operatorname {Hom}_\mathcal {E}(\textbf{1},T_i) \end{aligned}$$
(5.5)

is an isomorphism, for \(0\le i < p^n-1\). Indeed, \(T_i=0\) in \(\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2/I_n\) for \(i\ge p^n-1\), while \(I_n(\textbf{1}, T_i)=0\) for \(i<p^n-1\), see [2, Proposition 3.5] or [4]. So henceforth, we assume \(i<p^n-1\).

By definition, the morphism space

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {K}(\textbf{1}, T_i)\;\subset \; \operatorname {Hom}_{U_n}(\textbf{1}, T_i) \end{aligned}$$

is the space of all \(U_n\)-morphisms which factor through V. In particular, the dimension d of \(\mathcal {K}(\textbf{1},T_i)\) is the maximal d for which we have an embedding \(V^d\subset T_i\) (over \(U_n\)). In particular,

$$\begin{aligned} \dim _{\Bbbk }\mathcal {K}(\textbf{1}, T_i)= & \dim _{\Bbbk }\operatorname {Hom}_{U_n}(V,T_i)-\dim _{\Bbbk }\operatorname {Hom}_{U_n}(\textbf{1},T_i)\\= & \dim _{\Bbbk }\operatorname {Hom}_{U_n}(\textbf{1},T_i)-\dim _{\Bbbk }\operatorname {Hom}_{SL_2}(\textbf{1},T_i), \end{aligned}$$

where the second equality follows from Proposition 5.3.8. Consequently, we find

$$\begin{aligned} \dim _{\Bbbk }\operatorname {Hom}_{SL_2}(\textbf{1}, T_i)\;=\;\dim _{\Bbbk }\operatorname {Hom}_\mathcal {E}(\textbf{1},T_i), \end{aligned}$$

as required for Eq. 5.5 to be an isomorphism. To conclude the proof, we need to observe that a non-zero \(SL_2\)-morphism \(\textbf{1}\rightarrow T_i\), \(i<p^n-1\), cannot factor through \(\textbf{1}\hookrightarrow V\) over \(U_n\), which is clear from the treatment in the proof of Proposition 5.3.8. Indeed, images of the injective \(U_n\)-morphisms \(V\hookrightarrow T_i\) intersect trivially with the trivial \(SL_2\)-subrepresentation \(M_0\subset T_i\), whereas all \(SL_2\)-morphisms \(\textbf{1}\rightarrow T_i\) land in \(M_0\). \(\square \)

Remark 5.3.9

  1. (1)

    It is proved in [2, 6] that \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) is the monoidal abelian envelope of \(\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2/I_n\). Theorem 5.3.5 thus shows that \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) can now also be interpreted as the monoidal abelian envelope of \(\mathcal {D}/\mathcal {K}\), providing a definition of \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) purely in terms of \(C_p^n\) (and an arbitrary choice of faithful two-dimensional representation).

  2. (2)

    Theorem 5.3.5 shows in particular that

    $$\begin{aligned} (\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2)/I_n\;\rightarrow \; \operatorname {Stab}C_p^n \end{aligned}$$

    sends non-isomorphic objects to non-isomorphic objects and sends indecomposable objects to indecomposable objects. This was already observed in [1, Proposition 4.11] (for \(U_n=U(\mathbb {F}_{p^n})\)).

5.4 A conjectural \(\textbf{O}\)-functor

Fix \(n\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\), \({\underline{\lambda }}\in \mathbb {A}_f^n(\Bbbk )\) and set \(E=C_p^n\). In this section we give a partly conjectural construction of a family of \(\textbf{O}_n\)-functors. For \(p=2=n\) the necessary conjecture can easily be proved and those functors will be studied in detail in Sect. 7, after the necessary preparation in Sect. 6.

More concretely, Theorem 5.3.5 allows us to introduce an LSM functor \(\operatorname {Rep}E\supset \mathcal {D}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\rightarrow \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\), see (5.8) below. If we can extend this to a \(\textbf{V}\)-functor \(\operatorname {Rep}E\rightarrow \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\), then we can apply our general theory to construct an \(\textbf{O}_n^n\)-functor. As it happens, we can describe this potential \(\textbf{O}\)-functor (see Conjecture 5.4.2(3) below) even without knowing the extension exists, at the cost of not knowing whether the result is actually monoidal. This is the approach we take below.

5.4.1

We define a subfunctor

$$\begin{aligned} H_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\;\subset \; H^0(E,-):\operatorname {Rep}E\rightarrow \textrm{Vec},\quad M\mapsto \operatorname {Span}\{f(v)\mid f:V_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\rightarrow M\}, \end{aligned}$$

where \(v\in V_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\) spans the socle. In other words, \(H_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(M)\) corresponds to the radical of the trace of \(V_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\) in M, or most importantly, under the identification of \(H^0(E,-)\) and \(\operatorname {Hom}_{E}(\textbf{1},-)\), we can identify \(H_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(M)\) with the morphisms \(\textbf{1}\rightarrow M\) that factor via \(V_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\), so that

$$ H_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(M)\;=\; \mathcal {K}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(\textbf{1},M), \quad \text {for }M\in \mathcal {D}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}. $$

In particular, for projective modules \(P\in \operatorname {Rep}E\),

$$\begin{aligned} H_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(P)=H^0(E,P), \end{aligned}$$

and we can define unambiguously a bilinear functor

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {Stab}E\,\times \, \operatorname {Rep}E\;\rightarrow \; \textrm{Vec},\quad (M,N)\mapsto H^0(E,M\otimes N)/H_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(M\otimes N). \end{aligned}$$

Theorem 5.3.5(1) then yields a bilinear functor

$$\begin{aligned} (\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2)/I_n\,\times \, \operatorname {Rep}E\;\rightarrow \; \textrm{Vec}. \end{aligned}$$

By restricting from \((\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2)/I_n\) to the full subcategory \(\operatorname {Tilt}^{[n]}SL_2\) from Sect. 2.3.1, using the equivalence with the category \(\mathcal {P}\) of projectives in \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) in Eq. 2.2, and taking duals, we arrive at the functor

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {P}^{\textrm{op}}\times \operatorname {Rep}E\;\rightarrow \; \textrm{Vec},\quad (P,M)\mapsto H^0(E,R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(P^*)\otimes M)/H_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(P^*)\otimes M), \end{aligned}$$
(5.6)

where, by abuse of notation, we use the symbol P also for the corresponding \(SL_2\)-tilting module. For example, restricting Equation (5.6) to \(M\in \mathcal {D}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\subset \operatorname {Rep}E\) yields

$$\begin{aligned} (P,M)\mapsto \operatorname {Hom}_E(R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(P), M)/\mathcal {K}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(P), M)=\operatorname {Hom}_{\mathcal {D}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}/\mathcal {K}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}}(R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(P),M). \end{aligned}$$
(5.7)

Now the functor in Equation (5.6) can be reinterpreted as

$$\begin{aligned} \Theta ^{{\underline{\lambda }}}\;:\; \operatorname {Rep}E\;\rightarrow \; \operatorname {Fun}_{\Bbbk }(\mathcal {P}^{\textrm{op}},\textrm{Vec})\simeq \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}, \end{aligned}$$

and by Equation (5.7), \(\Theta ^{{\underline{\lambda }}}\) restricted to \(\mathcal {D}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\subset \operatorname {Rep}E\), yields the composite symmetric monoidal functor

$$\begin{aligned} F:\;\mathcal {D}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\;\rightarrow \; \mathcal {D}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}/\mathcal {K}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\xrightarrow {\sim } (\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2)/I_n{\mathop {\hookrightarrow }\limits ^{\Sigma ^n}}\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\end{aligned}$$
(5.8)

where the first functor is just projection onto the quotient and the second functor is a quasi-inverse of the equivalence in Theorem 5.3.5(2).

Conjecture 5.4.2

  1. (1)

    For an arbitrary \(M\in \operatorname {Rep}E\), the module

    $$\begin{aligned} R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(St_{n-1})\otimes M \end{aligned}$$

    belongs to \(\mathcal {D}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\).

  2. (2)

    The linear functor \(\Theta ^{{\underline{\lambda }}}:\operatorname {Rep}E\rightarrow \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\), defined in Sect. 5.4.1, has a symmetric monoidal structure which extends the symmetric monoidal structure of F in Equation (5.8).

  3. (3)

    The collection of \(\operatorname {Frob}^n\)-linear functors

    $$\begin{aligned} \Phi ^{{\underline{\lambda }}}_{\mathcal {C}}:\mathcal {C}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\simeq \operatorname {Fun}_{\Bbbk }(\mathcal {P}^{\textrm{op}},\mathcal {C}),\quad X\mapsto F_X \end{aligned}$$

    with

    $$\begin{aligned} F_X(P)=H^0\left( E,R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(P^*)\otimes _{\Bbbk } X^{\otimes p^n}\right) / H_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\left( R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(P^*)\otimes _{\Bbbk } X^{\otimes p^n}\right) \end{aligned}$$

    forms an \(\textbf{O}^n_n\)-functor. Here we abuse notation in identifying projective objects in \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) with \(SL_2\)-tilting modules via equivalence (2.2).

Theorem 5.4.3

We have the implications \((1)\Rightarrow (2)\Rightarrow (3)\) between the statements in Conjecture 5.4.2.

Before we prove the theorem, we make some comments and preparations.

Remark 5.4.4

  1. (1)

    If \(p=2=n\) and \({\underline{\lambda }}\in \mathbb {A}^2_f\), we set \(\lambda :=\lambda _2/\lambda _1\in \Bbbk \backslash \mathbb {F}_2\). Then \(R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(St_1)\) is isomorphic to \(A_1(\lambda )\) from Sect. 6.1.1 and Conjecture 5.4.2 follows immediately from Lemma 6.2.1 below. More substantial evidence for the conjecture will be given in future work.

  2. (2)

    Potentially, Conjecture 5.4.2(3) is weaker than Conjecture 5.4.2(1) or (2) due to Remark 5.2.6. Indeed, to prove (3) it would be sufficient to show that (1) is true only for all \(M\in \operatorname {Rep}E\) in the image of

    $$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {C}\rightarrow \operatorname {Rep}S_{p^n}\xrightarrow {\operatorname {Res}^{S_{p^n}}_E}\operatorname {Rep}E \end{aligned}$$

    for all tensor categories \(\mathcal {C}\).

In the following lemma, by a ‘thick tensor ideal’ in \(\operatorname {Rep}E\) we mean a collection of objects, closed under taking direct sums and summands, which is also closed under taking tensor products with arbitrary representations in \(\operatorname {Rep}E\).

Lemma 5.4.5

Conjecture 5.4.2(1) is valid if and only if the full subcategory of \(\operatorname {Rep}E\) comprising the image under \(R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\) of direct sums of copies of \(T_i\) with \(i\ge p^{n-1}-1\) is a thick tensor ideal in \(\operatorname {Rep}E\).

Proof

Clearly, the property in the lemma implies Conjecture 5.4.2(1). On the other hand, assume Conjecture 5.4.2(1) is valid. Let \(T\in \operatorname {Tilt}SL_2\) be a direct sum of copies of \(T_i,i\ge p^{n-1}-1\) and set \(S=St_{n-1}\). By the ideal structure recalled in Sect. 2.3.1, T is a summand of \(S\otimes T'\) for some \(T'\in \operatorname {Tilt}SL_2\). Moreover S, as a self-dual representation, is a summand of \(S\otimes S\otimes S\). Hence we can write T as a summand of \(S\otimes S\otimes T''\) (with \(T''=T'\otimes S\))

For any arbitrary \(M\in \operatorname {Rep}E\), it follows that \(R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(T)\otimes M\) is a summand of

$$\begin{aligned} R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(T''\otimes S)\otimes R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(S)\otimes M\simeq R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(T''\otimes S)\otimes R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(T_1)\simeq R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(T''\otimes T_1 \otimes S), \end{aligned}$$

for some \(T_1\in \operatorname {Tilt}SL_2\), where the first isomorphism is application of Conjecture 5.4.2(1). Again by the ideal structure of \(\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2\), the right-hand side is again in the full subcategory claimed to be an ideal in the lemma. \(\square \)

For a morphism \(u:U\rightarrow \textbf{1}\) in an LSM category, we define the morphism

$$\begin{aligned} u_\Delta :\;U\otimes U\xrightarrow {u\otimes U-U\otimes u}U. \end{aligned}$$

Lemma 5.4.6

Consider an LSM pseudo-abelian monoidal category \(\widetilde{\mathcal {A}}\) with full monoidal subcategory \(\mathcal {A}\). Consider an LSM functor \(F:\mathcal {A}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\) to a tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\) and a morphism \(f:X\rightarrow \textbf{1}\) in \(\mathcal {A}\) with \(F(f)\not =0\). Assume that for every \(Y\in \widetilde{\mathcal {A}}\), the object \(X\otimes Y\) belongs to \(\mathcal {A}\). Then there is a unique (up to isomorphism) LSM functor

$$\begin{aligned} \widetilde{F}\;:\; \widetilde{\mathcal {A}}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\end{aligned}$$

which restricts to F on \(\mathcal {A}\). The underlying \(\Bbbk \)-linear functor of \(\widetilde{F}\) is given by

$$\begin{aligned} \widetilde{F}(Y)\;=\; \operatorname {coker}F(Y\otimes f_\Delta ). \end{aligned}$$

Proof

Observe first that, for any morphism \(u:U\rightarrow \textbf{1}\) in a tensor category, the sequence

$$\begin{aligned} U\otimes U\xrightarrow {u_\Delta } U\xrightarrow {u}\textbf{1}\rightarrow 0 \end{aligned}$$

is (right) exact, see [7, Theorem 4.2.2(ii)]. In particular, with the \(\Bbbk \)-linear functor \(\widetilde{F}\) as defined in the lemma, it follows that for \(X\in \mathcal {A}\), we have natural isomorphisms

$$\begin{aligned} \widetilde{F}(X)\;\simeq \; \operatorname {coker}(F(X)\otimes F(f)_{\Delta })\;\simeq \; F(X), \end{aligned}$$

where we also used exactness of the tensor product in \(\mathcal {C}\).

We can give a monoidal structure on \(\tilde{F}\) as follows. First we can observe that for any \(A,Y\in \widetilde{\mathcal {A}}\), the above displayed isomorphisms and the fact that \(A\otimes X\otimes Y\simeq (A\otimes Y)\otimes X\in \mathcal {A}\), yield a natural isomorphism

$$\begin{aligned} F(A\otimes X)\otimes \widetilde{F}(Y)\;\simeq \;\operatorname {coker}F(A\otimes X\otimes Y\otimes f_\Delta )\;\simeq \;F(A\otimes X\otimes Y). \end{aligned}$$

For \(Y_1,Y_2\in \widetilde{\mathcal {A}}\), we thus obtain natural isomorphisms

$$\begin{aligned} \widetilde{F}(Y_1)\otimes \widetilde{F}(Y_2)\;\simeq \; \operatorname {coker}\left( F(Y_1\otimes f_\Delta )\otimes \widetilde{F}(Y_2)\right) \;\simeq \; \operatorname {coker}F(Y_1\otimes f_\Delta \otimes Y_2), \end{aligned}$$

and thus by using the braiding

$$\begin{aligned} \widetilde{F}(Y_1)\otimes \widetilde{F}(Y_2)\;\simeq \; \operatorname {coker}\left( F(Y_1\otimes Y_2\otimes f_\Delta )\right) \;=\; \widetilde{F}(Y_1\otimes Y_2). \end{aligned}$$

It can be verified that these isomorphisms equip \(\widetilde{F}\) with a monoidal structure which extends the one on F. Uniqueness is verified using similar arguments. \(\square \)

Proof of Theorem 5.4.3

First we prove that (1) implies (2). We start with an application of Lemma 5.4.6. We set \(\widetilde{\mathcal {A}}=\operatorname {Rep}E\) and \(\mathcal {A}=\mathcal {D}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\). We have a non-zero morphism in \(\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2\)

$$\begin{aligned} f': T_{2p^{n-1}-2}\;\rightarrow \; \textbf{1}, \end{aligned}$$

see [4, Lemma 5.3.3], so we set \(f=R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(f')\) and \(X=R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(T_{2p^{n-1}-2})\). Finally, we consider the composite LSM functor \(F:\mathcal {D}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\rightarrow \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) from Equation (5.8). Note that \(F(f)\not =0\), since by construction the image of f under the composite of the first two functors in Equation (5.8) is simply \(f'\), which is not contained in \(I_n\). Hence, by Lemma 5.4.5, under Conjecture 5.4.2(1), all assumptions in Lemma 5.4.6 are satisfied and we have the unique LSM extension

$$\begin{aligned} \widetilde{F}:\; \operatorname {Rep}E\rightarrow \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}. \end{aligned}$$

Now we show that \(\widetilde{F}\) is isomorphic to \(\Theta ^{{\underline{\lambda }}}\). For this we observe that for a projective object \(P\in \mathcal {P}\) in \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\), which is thus of the form \(\Sigma ^n(T)\) for \(T\in \operatorname {Tilt}^{[n]}SL_2\), and \(M\in \operatorname {Rep}E\), we have natural isomorphisms

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {Hom}_{\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}}(P,\widetilde{F}(M))\simeq & \operatorname {Hom}_{\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}}(\textbf{1}, P^*\otimes \widetilde{F}(M))\\\simeq & \operatorname {Hom}_{\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}}(\textbf{1}, F(R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(T^*))\otimes \widetilde{F}(M))\\\simeq & \operatorname {Hom}_{\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}}(\textbf{1}, F(R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(T^*)\otimes M))\\\simeq & \operatorname {Hom}_{E}(\textbf{1}, R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(T^*)\otimes M)/\mathcal {K}(\textbf{1},R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(T^*)\otimes M)\\\simeq & \operatorname {Hom}_{\operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}}(P,\Theta ^{{\underline{\lambda }}}(M)). \end{aligned}$$

Here, the first isomorphism is adjunction, the second is an application of Equation (5.8), the third uses Conjecture 5.4.2(1) and the fact that \(\widetilde{F}\) is monoidal and extends F, the fourth is an application of the equivalence in Theorem 5.3.5(2), while the last is the interpretation of \(\Theta ^{{\underline{\lambda }}}\) as being defined by Equation (5.6).

Now we prove that (2) implies (3) in Conjecture 5.4.2. Firstly we observe that \(\Theta ^{{\underline{\lambda }}}:\operatorname {Rep}E\rightarrow \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) is a \(\textbf{V}\)-functor. We thus need to show that \(\Theta ^{{\underline{\lambda }}}(\operatorname {Ind}^E_H\textbf{1})=0\) for all proper subgroups \(H<E\). Chasing through the definition of \(\Theta ^{{\underline{\lambda }}}\) (and using the ideal structure in \(\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2\)) it follows that it is sufficient to show that

$$\begin{aligned} R_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(St_{n-1})\otimes \operatorname {Ind}^E_H\textbf{1}\;\simeq \;\operatorname {Ind}^E_H\operatorname {Res}^E_HR_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(St_{n-1}) \end{aligned}$$

is projective. This follows since \(\operatorname {Res}^E_HR_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(St_{n-1})\) is projective for any proper subgroup \(H<E\). Indeed, \(\operatorname {Res}^E_HR_{{\underline{\lambda }}}(St_{n-1})\) is simply \(R_{{\underline{\lambda }}'}(St_{n-1})\) for some \({\underline{\lambda }}'\in \mathbb {A}^{m}_f(\Bbbk )\) with \(m<n\), so the conclusion follows from Theorem 5.3.5(1). Now the functor \(\Phi ^{{\underline{\lambda }}}_{\mathcal {C}}\) is constructed from \(\Theta ^{{\underline{\lambda }}}\) by the procedure in Theorem 5.2.1, concluding the proof. \(\square \)

Example 5.4.7

The definition of \(\Phi ^{{\underline{\lambda }}}_{\mathcal {C}}\) for \(n=1\) can be seen to be equivalent with the definition of \(\operatorname {Fr}\) in [5, §4.3].

6 The Klein 4-group

In this section we assume \(\operatorname {char}(\Bbbk )=2\). We gather and prove some results that are needed to establish Conjecture 5.4.2 for the case \(p=2=n\), and more generally explore the full potential for \(\textbf{O}\)-functors based on the transitive permutation group \(C_2^2<S_4\) using the formalism from Sect. 5.

6.1 Classifying LSM functors to tensor categories

6.1.1

Notation Recall, for instance from [3], that the indecomposable modules of \(\Bbbk C_2^2\) are classified as follows. For every \(i\in \mathbb {Z}\), we have the i-th Heller shift \(\Omega ^{i}\textbf{1}\). For instance, \(\Omega ^{-1}\textbf{1}\) is three-dimensional with simple top. Besides the indecomposable projective module, this leaves the (self-dual) indecomposable modules \(A_m(\lambda )\) with \(m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\) and \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\). For \(\lambda \in \Bbbk =\mathbb {A}^1(\Bbbk )\subset \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\), \(A_m(\lambda )\) is the 2m-dimensional module on which the generators act as

$$\begin{aligned} g_1\,\mapsto \,\left( \begin{array}{c|c} \mathbb {I}_m & 0 \\ \hline \mathbb {I}_m & \mathbb {I}_m \end{array}\right) \quad \text{ and }\quad g_2\,\mapsto \, \left( \begin{array}{c|c} \mathbb {I}_m & 0 \\ \hline \mathbb {J}_\lambda & \mathbb {I}_m \end{array}\right) , \end{aligned}$$
(6.1)

where \(\mathbb {I}_m\) is the \(m\times m\) identity matrix and \(\mathbb {J}_\lambda \) is an indecomposable Jordan block with generalised eigenvalue \(\lambda \). Finally, \(A_m(\infty )\) is \(A_m(0)\) but with the roles of the two generators reversed.

It will be useful for the sequel to fix, for every \(\mu \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\), a morphism \(f_\mu \) in \(\operatorname {Rep}C_2^2\), uniquely determined up to a (non-zero) scalar, which yields a short exact sequence

$$\begin{aligned} 0\rightarrow \textbf{1}\xrightarrow {f_\mu } \Omega ^{-1}\textbf{1}\rightarrow A_1(\mu )\rightarrow 0.\end{aligned}$$
(6.2)

Up to duality, this realises \(A_1(\mu )\) as a Carlson module.

Finally, we denote by \(\alpha _2\) the Frobenius kernel of the additive group \(\mathbb {G}_a\) and by \(\textrm{Vec}_{\mathbb {Z}}\) the tensor category of \(\mathbb {Z}\)-graded vector spaces, with ordinary braiding (making the forgetful functor to \(\textrm{Vec}\) symmetric monoidal).

Theorem 6.1.2

Every LSM functor from \(\operatorname {Rep}C_2^2\) to a tensor category is a composite of a tensor functor with (precisely one) of the following LSM functors.

  1. (0)

    The identity functor of \(\operatorname {Rep}C_2^2\).

  2. (1)

    For every \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\backslash \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\) a non-faithful LSM functor

    $$\begin{aligned} \Theta =\Theta ^\lambda _1\;:\;\operatorname {Rep}C_2^2\;\rightarrow \; \operatorname {Ver}_4, \end{aligned}$$

    uniquely determined by the property \(\Theta (A_1(\lambda ))\not =0\) (which is equivalent to the property \(\Theta (A_2(\lambda ))\not =0\)).

  3. (2)

    For every \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\) a non-faithful LSM functor

    $$\begin{aligned} \Theta =\Theta ^\lambda _0\;:\;\operatorname {Rep}C_2^2\;\rightarrow \; \operatorname {Rep}C_2, \end{aligned}$$

    uniquely determined by the property that \(\Theta (A_{1}(\lambda ))\) is projective.

  4. (3)

    For every \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\) and \(m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\), with \(m>1\) in case \(\lambda \not \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\), an LSM functor

    $$\begin{aligned} \Theta =\Theta ^\lambda _m\;:\;\operatorname {Rep}C_2^2\;\rightarrow \; \operatorname {Rep}\alpha _2, \end{aligned}$$

    uniquely determined by the properties that \(\Theta (A_m(\lambda ))=0\) and that \(\Theta (A_{m+1}(\lambda ))\) is projective.

  5. (4)

    For every \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\) an LSM functor

    $$\begin{aligned} \Theta =\Theta _\infty ^\lambda \;:\;\operatorname {Rep}C_2^2\;\rightarrow \; \textrm{Vec}, \end{aligned}$$

    uniquely determined by the properties \(\Theta (A_m(\mu ))=0\) for all \(\mu \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\) and \(m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\), and \(\Theta (f_\lambda )=0\) while \(\Theta (f_\mu )\not =0\) for some \(\mu \).

  6. (5)

    An LSM functor

    $$\begin{aligned} \Theta =\Theta _\infty =\Sigma \;:\;\operatorname {Rep}C_2^2\;\rightarrow \; \textrm{Vec}_{\mathbb {Z}}, \end{aligned}$$

    uniquely determined by the properties \(\Theta (f_\lambda )=0\) and \(\Theta (A_m(\lambda ))=0\) for all \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\) and \(m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\), and \(\Theta (\Omega ^1\textbf{1})\simeq \textbf{1}\langle 1\rangle \), the tensor unit in degree 1.

The proof of this theorem will occupy the rest of this section. First we observe that, since the modules of the form \(\operatorname {Ind}^{C_2^2}_H\textbf{1}\), for proper subgroups \(H<C_2^2\), are \(A_1(0)\), \(A_1(1)\), \(A_1(\infty )\) and \(kC_2^2\), we obtain the following corollary.

Corollary 6.1.3

Let \(C_2^2<S_4\) be the permutation group from Example 5.1.6(2). Every \(\textbf{V}\)-functor for this permutation group is a descendant (in the sense of Sect. 5.1) of one of the functors

$$\begin{aligned} \{\Theta ^\lambda _m\mid \lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk ), m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\cup \{\infty \}\}\cup \{\Theta _\infty \}. \end{aligned}$$

Remark 6.1.4

  1. (1)

    It follows from the tensor product rules in Lemma 6.2.1 below that \(\Theta ^\lambda _m(A_n(\mu ))=0\) when \(\mu \not =\lambda \) and, for \(\lambda \not \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\), that

    $$\begin{aligned} \Theta _1^\lambda (A_1(\lambda ))\;\simeq \; V\in \operatorname {Ver}_4. \end{aligned}$$
  2. (2)

    It also follows from Lemma 6.2.1 that \(\Theta _m^\lambda (A_n(\lambda ))\not =0\) if \(n>m\).

Remark 6.1.5

A neat pattern, for which the only evidence at the moment is Lemma 5.1.9 and Theorem 6.1.2, would be that the only LSM functors from \(\operatorname {Rep}C_p^r\) to incompressible tensor categories land in \(\operatorname {Ver}_{p^r}\).

6.2 Preparatory results

The following result can be found on page 82 of [3].

Lemma 6.2.1

With \(\lambda ,\mu \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\), we have the following tensor products in \(\operatorname {Stab}C_2^2\):

  1. (1)

    For \(m,n\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\), with \(m+n>2\),

    $$A_m(\lambda )\otimes A_n(\mu )\;\simeq \;{\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 0,& \text{ if } \lambda \not =\mu ;\\ A_{\min (m,n)}(\lambda )^2,& \text{ if } \lambda =\mu . \end{array}\right. }$$
  2. (2)
    $$A_1(\lambda )\otimes A_1(\mu )\;\simeq \;{\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 0,& \text{ if } \lambda \not =\mu ;\\ A_{2}(\lambda ),& \text{ if } \lambda =\mu \not \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2);\\ A_{1}(\lambda )^2,& \text{ if } \lambda =\mu \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2). \end{array}\right. }$$
  3. (3)

    For \(i,j\in \mathbb {Z}\), \(\Omega ^i\textbf{1}\otimes \Omega ^j\textbf{1}\;\simeq \; \Omega ^{i+j}\textbf{1}.\)

  4. (4)

    For \(i\in \mathbb {Z}\), \(m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\), \(A_m(\lambda )\otimes \Omega ^i\textbf{1}\;\simeq \; A_m(\lambda )\).

Lemma 6.2.2

Fix \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\) and \(m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\).

  1. (1)

    For \(1\le i\le m\), there is a unique submodule, and a unique quotient, of \(A_m(\lambda )\) isomorphic to \(A_i(\lambda )\).

  2. (2)

    The \(\operatorname {End}_{C^2_2}(A_m(\lambda ))\)-module \(\operatorname {Hom}_{C_2^2}(\textbf{1},A_m(\lambda ))\) has one-dimensional top, and its unique maximal submodule consists of the morphisms that factor via \(A_{m-1}(\lambda )\subset A_m(\lambda )\).

  3. (3)

    There is a \(\Bbbk \)-basis of \(\operatorname {End}_{C^2_2}(A_m(\lambda ))\) of the following form: one composition \(A_m(\lambda )\twoheadrightarrow A_i(\lambda )\hookrightarrow A_m(\lambda )\) for each \(1\le i\le m\) and \(m^2\) compositions \(A_m(\lambda )\twoheadrightarrow \textbf{1}\hookrightarrow A_m(\lambda )\)

Proof

Part (1) follows from the description of \(A_m(\lambda )\) in Equation (6.1).

For part (2), set \(R=\operatorname {End}_{C^2_2}(A_m(\lambda ))\) and \(T=\operatorname {Hom}_{C_2^2}(\textbf{1},A_m(\lambda ))\). Since R is a local algebra, finite-dimensional over an algebraically closed field, it suffices to show that all vectors that are not in the subspace

$$\begin{aligned} T_1:=\operatorname {Hom}_{C_2^2}(\textbf{1}, A_{m-1}(\lambda ))\;\subset \; \operatorname {Hom}_{C_2^2}(\textbf{1}, A_{m}(\lambda ))=T, \end{aligned}$$

defined via \(A_{m-1}(\lambda )\subset A_m(\lambda )\) from part (1), generate T as an R-module. Note that \(\dim T=m\) and \(\dim T_1=m-1\). For \(v\in T\backslash T_1\), we consider the composite

$$\begin{aligned} \textbf{1}\xrightarrow {v} A_m(\lambda )\twoheadrightarrow A_{m-1}(\lambda )\hookrightarrow A_m(\lambda ), \end{aligned}$$

where the second and the third morphism come from part (1) and its dual. Clearly, this composite is in \(T_1\), but it also can be seen that it is not included in the codimension 2 subspace \(\operatorname {Hom}_{C_2^2}(\textbf{1},A_{m-2}(\lambda ))\) of T. Continuing this procedure shows that \(Rv=T\).

For part (3), the case \(m=1\) is straightforward, so we assume \(m>1\). Lemma 6.2.1(1) implies that

$$\begin{aligned} A_m(\lambda )^{\otimes 2}\;\simeq \; A_m(\lambda )^2\oplus (\Bbbk C_2^2)^{m^2-m}. \end{aligned}$$

Hence, by adjunction, the proposed basis has the correct size, and it suffices to show that we can choose a linearly independent set of such morphisms, which is obvious by part (1). \(\square \)

The following lemma is trivial, but it will be useful to have it written out.

Lemma 6.2.3

For a self-dual object Y satisfying \(Y^{\otimes 2}\simeq Y^2\) in an additive monoidal category, we have canonical isomorphisms of vector spaces

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {End}(Y)\simeq \operatorname {Hom}(\textbf{1}, Y)^2\simeq \operatorname {Hom}(Y,\textbf{1})^2. \end{aligned}$$

Lemma 6.2.4

Consider \(A_m(\lambda )\in \operatorname {Rep}C_2^2\) with \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\) and \(m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\), excluding the case \(m=1\) for \(\lambda \not \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\). Denote by \(\mathcal {B}=\mathcal {B}_m(\lambda )\) the additive (rigid) monoidal subcategory of \(\operatorname {Stab}C_2^2\) generated by \(A_m(\lambda )\).

  1. (1)

    There is precisely one tensor ideal \(\mathcal {I}\) in \(\mathcal {B}\) that does not contain \(A_m(\lambda )\) and that is the kernel of an LSM functor to a tensor category.

  2. (2)

    The ideal \(\mathcal {I}\) in part (1) is the maximal tensor ideal in \(\mathcal {B}\) that does not contain \(A_m(\lambda )\). It does not contain all morphisms \(A_m(\lambda )\rightarrow \textbf{1}\).

  3. (3)

    The symmetric monoidal category \(\mathcal {B}/\mathcal {I}\) is a tensor category, concretely

    $$\mathcal {B}/\mathcal {I}\;\simeq \;{\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \operatorname {Rep}C_2,& \text{ if } m=1 \text{(and } \lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)),\\ \operatorname {Ver}_4^+,& \text{ if } m=2 \text{ and } \lambda \not \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2),\\ \operatorname {Rep}\alpha _2,& \text{ otherwise }. \end{array}\right. }$$

Proof

Set \(X=A_m(\lambda )\). By Lemma 6.2.1(1) and (2), in \(\mathcal {B}\subset \operatorname {Stab}C_2^2\) we have

$$\begin{aligned} X\otimes X\;\simeq \; X\oplus X. \end{aligned}$$
(6.3)

In particular, the objects in \(\mathcal {B}\subset \operatorname {Stab}C_2^2\) are direct sums of copies of \(\textbf{1}\) and X.

Let Y be a non-zero image of X in some tensor category \(\mathcal {V}\) under an LSM functor. By Lemma 6.2.3, Y admits non-zero morphisms to and from \(\textbf{1}\). In particular, in the Grothendieck ring \(K_0(\mathcal {V})\), we have \([Y]=[Z]+[\textbf{1}]\) for some \(Z\in \mathcal {V}\). Equation (6.3) shows that in \(K_0(\mathcal {V})\):

$$\begin{aligned} ([Z]+1)^2\;=\; 2[Z]+2\quad \Rightarrow \quad [Z]^2=1, \end{aligned}$$

so that Y must either be a self-extension (possibly split) of \(\textbf{1}\), or a direct sum of \(\textbf{1}\) with an invertible object.

The insight from the previous paragraph shows that for any tensor ideal J for which \(\mathcal {B}/J\) admits a faithful LSM functor to a tensor category \(\mathcal {V}\), we must have either

$$\begin{aligned} \dim \operatorname {Hom}_\mathcal {B}(\textbf{1},X)\;=\; 1+\dim J(\textbf{1},X), \end{aligned}$$
(6.4)

or alternatively (and forcing \(Y\simeq \textbf{1}^2\))

$$\begin{aligned} \dim \operatorname {Hom}_\mathcal {B}(\textbf{1},X)\;=\; 2+\dim J(\textbf{1},X).\end{aligned}$$
(6.5)

In the case of Equation (6.5), the functor \(\mathcal {B}/J\rightarrow \mathcal {V}\) is fully faithful, for instance by Lemma 6.2.3, so that the algebra \(\operatorname {End}_{\mathcal {B}/J}(X)\simeq \operatorname {End}_{\mathcal {V}}(\textbf{1}^2)\) must be the matrix algebra \(\textrm{Mat}_2(\Bbbk )\), which is impossible since \(\operatorname {End}_{\mathcal {B}}(X)\) is local.

By a direct application of [4, Proposition 3.2.1], we have an inclusion preserving bijection between proper tensor ideals in \(\mathcal {B}\) and \(\operatorname {End}_{\mathcal {B}}(X)\)-submodules of \(M:=\operatorname {Hom}_\mathcal {B}(\textbf{1},X)\). We have

$$\begin{aligned} M\simeq \operatorname {Hom}_{C_2^2}(\textbf{1}, A_m(\lambda )), \end{aligned}$$

and Lemma 6.2.2(2) thus implies that there is a unique tensor ideal J in \(\mathcal {B}\) for which Equation (6.4) is satisfied. Moreover, this is the maximal tensor ideal which does not contain all morphisms \(\textbf{1}\rightarrow X\), which, by Lemma 6.2.3, is the maximal tensor ideal that does not contain X. We call this ideal \(\mathcal {J}\).

We have thus far proved uniqueness of the ideal in (1), and that this hypothetical ideal would have to satisfy the two properties in (2). To conclude the proof we demonstrate that (3) holds for the ideal \(\mathcal {J}\), which then implies (1) too.

In \(\mathcal {B}/\mathcal {J}\), we have unique (up to scalars) non-zero morphisms \(\alpha :\textbf{1}\rightarrow X\) and \(\beta :X\rightarrow \textbf{1}\). Moreover, \(\operatorname {End}_{\mathcal {B}/\mathcal {J}}(X)\) is 2-dimensional by Equation (6.3) and Lemma 6.2.3. We can observe that \(\beta \circ \alpha =0\) in \(\mathcal {B}/\mathcal {J}\), as that is already the case in \(\operatorname {Rep}C_2^2\). Furthermore, we claim \(\alpha \circ \beta \not =0\). Indeed, we can consider the basis in Lemma 6.2.2(3) and claim that all endomorphisms \(A_m(\lambda )\twoheadrightarrow A_i(\lambda )\hookrightarrow A_m(\lambda )\), for \(i<m\) are zero in \(\mathcal {B}/\mathcal {J}\). If not, then by adjunction and Lemma 6.2.1 there would be a composite morphism \(\textbf{1}\rightarrow A_i(\lambda )^2\rightarrow A_m(\lambda )^2\) which is not in \(\mathcal {J}\). By Lemma 6.2.2(2), such morphisms \(\textbf{1}\rightarrow A_m(\lambda )\) are in \(\mathcal {J}\). Hence, some composite morphism \(A_m(\lambda )\twoheadrightarrow \textbf{1}\hookrightarrow A_m(\lambda )\) must not be sent to zero in \(\mathcal {B}/\mathcal {J}\), which implies \(\alpha \circ \beta \not =0\).

It thus follows that \(\mathcal {B}/\mathcal {J}\) is \(\Bbbk \)-linearly equivalent with \(\Bbbk [x]/x^2\text{-mod }\), which implies that \(\mathcal {B}/\mathcal {J}\) is abelian and hence a tensor category. By [15, Corollary 2.20], \(\mathcal {B}/\mathcal {J}\) must be one of the tensor categories in (3).

To decide which of the three tensor categories we obtain for every given pair \((\lambda ,m)\), we can use Remark 6.2.5 below, which reduces the problem to a tedious computation which we omit. A considerable amount can actually be avoided. Indeed, the case \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\), \(m=1\) follows immediately from three inclusions \(\operatorname {Rep}C_2\subset \operatorname {Stab}C_2^2\) coming from the three epimorphisms \(C_2^2\twoheadrightarrow C_2\). The case \(\lambda \not \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\), \(m=2\) follows from Theorem 5.3.5(2) and [1, Remark 3.10]. For the remaining cases, one can use the functors in Sect. 6.3.1 and Sect. 6.3.2 to demonstrate that \(\mathcal {B}/\mathcal {I}\) must be tannakian, eliminating the possibility \(\operatorname {Ver}_4^+\). \(\square \)

Remark 6.2.5

The categories \(\operatorname {Rep}C_2\), \(\operatorname {Rep}\alpha _2\) and \(\operatorname {Ver}_4^+\) are given by \(\Bbbk [x]/x^2\text{-mod }\) as \(\Bbbk \)-linear categories. Furthermore, for the P the regular module, we have in all three categories

$$\begin{aligned} P\otimes P\;\simeq \; P\oplus P. \end{aligned}$$

A convenient way to tell the three tensor categories apart is by considering the action of \(1+\sigma \in \Bbbk S_2\) (with \(\sigma \) the generator of \(S_2\)) via the braiding on \(P^{\otimes 2}\). The action is (up to conjugation by \(GL_2(\Bbbk [x]/x^2)\)) given by the following elements of \(\textrm{Mat}_2(\Bbbk [x]/x^2)\simeq \operatorname {End}(P^2)\)

$$\left( \begin{array}{cc} x & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{array}\right) ,\quad \left( \begin{array}{cc} 0 & 0 \\ x & 0 \end{array}\right) ,\quad \text{ and }\quad \left( \begin{array}{cc} 0 & x \\ x & 0 \end{array}\right) $$

in \(\operatorname {Rep}C_2\), \(\operatorname {Rep}\alpha _2\) and \(\operatorname {Ver}_4^+\) respectively. In other words, the first case is the only case with non-zero trace and the last case is the only one for which the corresponding multiplication operator (which squares to zero) has zero cohomology.

6.3 Proof of Theorem 6.1.2

Let \(\Theta :\operatorname {Rep}C_2^2\rightarrow \mathcal {V}\) be an LSM functor to a tensor category \(\mathcal {V}\). If \(\Theta \) is faithful, then it is exact by Theorem 2.2.1 and therefore a tensor functor. Faithful functors thus correspond to those in Theorem 6.1.2(0) and henceforth we can restrict to non-faithful functors. Since the projective modules are contained in each tensor ideal, we are thus interested in LSM functors

$$\begin{aligned} \Theta :\;\operatorname {Stab}C_2^2\;\rightarrow \;\mathcal {V}. \end{aligned}$$

We start by considering the following 4 options 6.3.1 – 6.3.4.

6.3.1

Assume \(\Theta (A_2(\lambda ))\not =0\) for some \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\backslash \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\)

Denote by \(\mathcal {A}\) the full additive monoidal subcategory of \(\operatorname {Stab}C_2^2\) generated by \(A_1(\lambda )\). By Lemma 6.2.1,

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {A}\;\subset \;\widetilde{\mathcal {A}}\;:=\;\operatorname {Stab}C_2^2 \end{aligned}$$

comprises direct sums of \(\textbf{1}\), \(A_1(\lambda )\) and \(A_2(\lambda )\) and satisfies the hypothesis in Lemma 5.4.6, for \(X:=A_2(\lambda )\).

Furthermore, by Lemma 6.2.3, there must be a morphism \(A_2(\lambda )\rightarrow \textbf{1}\) which is not sent to zero by \(\Theta \). By Lemma 5.4.6, restriction yields a correspondence between LSM functors \(\operatorname {Stab}C_2^2\rightarrow \mathcal {V}\) that do not kill \(A_2(\lambda )\) and LSM functors \(\mathcal {A}\rightarrow \mathcal {V}\) with the same condition.

Moreover, if we set \(B:=\Theta (A_1(\lambda ))\in \mathcal {V}\), then Lemma 6.2.1 implies

$$\begin{aligned} B^{\otimes 3}\;\simeq \; B\oplus B. \end{aligned}$$

Such objects B cannot contain \(\textbf{1}\) as a subobject. In fact, they must be simple as they have growth dimension \(\sqrt{2}<2\). Consequently, \(\Theta \) must send all morphisms \(\textbf{1}\rightarrow A_1(\lambda )\) to zero.

Setting \({\underline{\lambda }}=(1:\lambda )\), we can observe that \(\mathcal {A}\) is precisely the image of \(\mathcal {D}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}\) from Sect. 5.3 in the stable category. By the previous paragraph, LSM functors \(\mathcal {A}\rightarrow \mathcal {V}\) thus correspond to LSM functors \(\mathcal {D}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}/\mathcal {K}\rightarrow \mathcal {V}\), with \(\mathcal {K}\) also as in Sect. 5.3. Applying Theorem 5.3.5(2) yields

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {D}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}/\mathcal {K}\;\simeq \; (\operatorname {Tilt}SL_2)/I_2\;\simeq \; \operatorname {Ver}_4,\end{aligned}$$
(6.6)

where the last equivalence is in [1, Remark 3.10]. This equivalence exchanges \(A_2(\lambda )\) and the projective cover of \(\textbf{1}\) in \(\operatorname {Ver}_4\).

Since \(A_2(\lambda )\) is projective in the tensor category \(\operatorname {Ver}_4\), Lemma 2.2.2 shows that all LSM functors \(\mathcal {D}_{{\underline{\lambda }}}/\mathcal {K}\rightarrow \mathcal {V}\) that do not kill \(A_2(\lambda )\) are (faithful) tensor functors. In conclusion, all non-faithful LSM functors \(\Theta \) from \(\operatorname {Rep}C_2^2\) to tensor categories satisfying \(\Theta (A_2(\lambda ))\not =0\) factor through a unique functor as in Theorem 6.1.2(1).

6.3.2

\(\Theta (A_1(\lambda ))\not =0\) for some \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\)

We freely use Lemma 6.2.1. Observe that non-zero morphisms \(A_1(\lambda )\rightarrow \textbf{1}\) are not annihilated by \(\Theta \), due to Lemma 6.2.3. By Lemma 5.4.6, LSM functors \(\operatorname {Stab}C_2^2\rightarrow \mathcal {V}\) which do not kill \(A_1(\lambda )\) are thus in natural bijection with LSM functors \(\mathcal {A}\rightarrow \mathcal {V}\) that do not kill \(A_1(\lambda )\), where \(\mathcal {A}\simeq \operatorname {Rep}C_2\) is the monoidal subcategory of \(\operatorname {Stab}C_2^2\) generated by \(A_1(\lambda )\). It then follows from Lemma 2.2.2 that such functors factor through a unique functor as in Theorem 6.1.2(3).

Note that these three (for \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\)) functors are of the form

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {Rep}C_2^2\simeq (\operatorname {Rep}C_2)\boxtimes (\operatorname {Rep}C_2)\xrightarrow {(\operatorname {Rep}C_2)\boxtimes \Sigma } (\operatorname {Rep}C_2)\boxtimes \textrm{Vec}\simeq \operatorname {Rep}C_2, \end{aligned}$$

where we carried out semisimplification of one of the three subgroups \(C_2<C_2^2\).

6.3.3

\(\Theta (A_m(\lambda ))=0\) and \(\Theta (A_{m+1}(\lambda ))\not =0\) for some \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\), \(m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\)

Firstly, we can observe that the two conditions become contradictory for \(m=1\) and \(\lambda \not \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\), by Lemma 6.2.1(2).

For the remainder of this subsection we focus on the case \(\lambda \not \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\) (and \(m>1\)), as the case \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\) can similarly be derived from Section 6.3.2. We claim that any \(\Theta \) with the stated properties factors uniquely through one such LSM functor \(\operatorname {Stab}C_2^2\rightarrow \operatorname {Rep}\alpha _2\).

We set \(l=m+1\) for convenience. Consider the monoidal subcategory \(\mathcal {B}=\mathcal {B}_l(\lambda )\subset \operatorname {Stab}C_2^2\) from Lemma 6.2.4 with indecomposable objects \(\textbf{1}\) and \(A_l(\lambda )\). Let J denote the ideal in \(\mathcal {B}\) which is the kernel of

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {B}\hookrightarrow \operatorname {Stab}C_2^2\twoheadrightarrow (\operatorname {Rep}C_2^2)/I \end{aligned}$$

with I the tensor ideal in \(\operatorname {Rep}C_2^2\) generated by \(A_{l-1}(\lambda )\).

As in Sect. 6.3.1 and Sect. 6.3.2, it follows from Lemma 5.4.6, applied to \(\widetilde{\mathcal {A}}=(\operatorname {Rep}C_2^2)/I\) and \(\mathcal {A}=\mathcal {B}/J\) that it suffices to show that there is a unique LSM functor \(\mathcal {B}/J\rightarrow \operatorname {Rep}\alpha _2\) such that all LSM functors \(\mathcal {B}/J\rightarrow \mathcal {V}\) to tensor categories \(\mathcal {V}\) that do not annihilate \(A_l(\lambda )\) factor via the former.

Now, since the ideal I does not contain \(A_{l}(\lambda )\), we find \(J\subset \mathcal {I}\), for \(\mathcal {I}\) the unique ideal in \(\mathcal {B}\) from Lemma 6.2.4. By this lemma (and the fact that \(\operatorname {Rep}\alpha _2\) does not have non-trivial auto-equivalences), it now suffices to observe that the tensor category \(\mathcal {B}/\mathcal {I}\) is \(\operatorname {Rep}\alpha _2\), by Lemma 6.2.4(3).

6.3.4

\(\Theta (A_n(\mu ))=0\) for all \(n\ge 1\) and \(\mu \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\) The only remaining indecomposable objects in \(\operatorname {Stab}C_2^2\) are \(\Omega ^i\textbf{1}\) for \(i\in \mathbb {Z}\). These are invertible, see Lemma 6.2.1(3). Every morphism \(\textbf{1}\rightarrow \Omega ^i\textbf{1}\), for \(i>0\), must be sent to zero by \(\Theta \), since they factor as \(\textbf{1}\rightarrow A_i(0)\rightarrow \Omega ^i\textbf{1}\).

Next assume that all morphisms \(\textbf{1}\rightarrow \Omega ^{-1}\textbf{1}\) are sent to zero by \(\Theta \). Since all morphisms \(\textbf{1}\rightarrow \Omega ^{-i}\textbf{1}\), for \(i>1\), are linear combinations of composites \(\textbf{1}\rightarrow \Omega ^{-1}\textbf{1}\rightarrow \Omega ^{-i}\textbf{1}\), they all go to zero, too. It thus follows that \(\Theta \) kills all morphisms between indecomposables that are not isomorphisms, and \(\Theta \) factors through the semisimplification \(\overline{\operatorname {Rep}C_2^2}\), which is the category of \(\mathbb {Z}\)-graded vector spaces. This leads to composite functors with the one in Theorem 6.1.2(5).

Since the space of morphisms \(\textbf{1}\rightarrow \Omega ^{-1}\textbf{1}\) is two-dimensional, and must be sent by \(\Theta \) to a morphism space between invertible objects in a tensor category, the alternative is that the space of morphisms \(\textbf{1}\rightarrow \Omega ^{-1}\textbf{1}\) that are sent to zero by \(\Theta \) is spanned by \(f_\lambda \) for some \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\). Let J denote the tensor ideal in \(\operatorname {Rep}C_2^2\) generated by all \(A_m(\mu )\), all morphisms \(\textbf{1}\rightarrow \Omega ^i\textbf{1}\), \(i>0\), and \(f_\lambda \). It follows that all morphism spaces from \(\textbf{1}\) to indecomposable objects in \(\mathcal {A}:=(\operatorname {Rep}C_2^2)/J\) are zero, except that

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {A}(\textbf{1}, \Omega ^{-i}\textbf{1})\;\simeq \;\Bbbk ,\quad \text{ for } \;i\ge 0. \end{aligned}$$

Any LSM functor \(\mathcal {A}\rightarrow \mathcal {V}\) to a tensor category \(\mathcal {V}\) that does not kill all morphisms \(\textbf{1}\rightarrow \Omega ^{-1}\textbf{1}\) lands in \(\textrm{Vec}\subset \mathcal {V}\), and there is a unique faithful LSM functor \(\mathcal {A}\rightarrow \textrm{Vec}\). Hence, the assumptions in the current paragraph lead to functors as in Theorem 6.1.2(4).

6.3.5

Conclusion Now let \(\Theta \) be any LSM functor from \(\operatorname {Stab}C_2^2\) to a tensor category. It follows from Lemma 6.2.1(1) that \(\Theta (A_m(\mu ))=0\) for all \(\mu \) or for all \(\mu \not =\lambda \) for one \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\). Moreover, if \(\Theta (A_{m+1}(\lambda ))=0\) then \(\Theta (A_m(\lambda ))=0\), by Lemma 6.2.1(1). We must therefore be in one of the cases 6.3.1 – 6.3.4. This completes the proof of Theorem 6.1.2.

We conclude this section with the following consequences of the proof of Theorem 6.1.2. We denote by \(\mathcal {F}\) the \(\Bbbk \)-linear symmetric rigid monoidal category of finite-dimensional \(\mathbb {Z}\)-filtered vector spaces, with filtration respecting morphisms. Below we consider the LSM functors to \(\textrm{Vec}_{\mathbb {Z}}\) and \(\textrm{Vec}\) which associate to a filtered vector space its associated graded vector space or forget the filtration, respectively.

Lemma 6.3.6

For every \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\), there exists an LSM functor \(F_\lambda \), admitting a commutative diagram

Proof

Let \(\mathcal {A}\) be as in Sect. 6.3.4. One can verify that any two non-zero morphisms between indecomposable objects (i.e. the \(\Omega ^j\textbf{1}\)) in \(\mathcal {A}\) compose to non-zero morphisms. We may thus identify \(\mathcal {A}\) with \(\mathcal {F}\). \(\square \)

For \(m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\cup \{\infty \}\), denote by \(J_m^\lambda \) the tensor ideal in \(\operatorname {Rep}C_2^2\) that is the kernel of \(\Theta _m^\lambda \). Note that the kernel \(J_\infty \) of \(\Theta _\infty \) is the unique maximal tensor ideal, the ideal of negligible morphisms \(\mathcal {N}\).

Lemma 6.3.7

For every \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\), we have a chain of strict inclusions

$$\begin{aligned} J_1^\lambda \subset J_2^\lambda \subset J_3^\lambda \subset \cdots \subset J_\infty ^\lambda \subset J_\infty =\mathcal {N}. \end{aligned}$$

Proof

Firstly, it is clear from the formulation of Theorem 6.1.2 that there are no equalities between these ideals.

To prove that \(J_m^\lambda \subset J^\lambda _\infty \), by Sect. 6.3.4 it is sufficient to show that \(J_m^\lambda \) does not contain \(f_\mu \) for \(\mu \not =\lambda \). Consider therefore the short exact sequence in Equation (6.2) for any \(\mu \not =\lambda \) and the corresponding exact triangle in \(\operatorname {Stab}C_2^2\). By taking the tensor product with \(A_{m+1}(\lambda )\), we obtain by Lemma 6.2.1 an exact triangle

$$\begin{aligned} A_{m+1}(\lambda )\;\xrightarrow {f_\mu \otimes A_{m+1}(\lambda )} A_{m+1}(\lambda )\;\rightarrow \; 0\;\rightarrow , \end{aligned}$$

showing that \(f_\mu \otimes A_{m+1}(\lambda )\) is an isomorphism in \(\operatorname {Stab}C_2^2\). It thus follows indeed that \(\Theta _m^\lambda (f_\mu \otimes A_1(\lambda ))\) is not zero.

That \(J_m^\lambda \subset J_{m+1}^\lambda \) can be seen as follows. For any m, the morphisms \(\textbf{1}\rightarrow \Omega ^j\textbf{1}\) in \(J_m^\lambda \) are the same as in \(J^\lambda _\infty \). All morphisms \(\textbf{1}\rightarrow A_n(\mu )\) are in \(J_m^\lambda \) when \(\mu \not =\lambda \). Finally, the space of morphisms \(\textbf{1}\rightarrow A_n(\lambda )\) in \(J_m^\lambda \) is always of codimension zero or one, so this space is either everything or the subspace from Lemma 6.2.2(2). Furthermore, the codimension is zero if and only if \(A_n(\lambda )\) is sent to zero (except for \(n=1\) and \(\lambda \not \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\), in which case it is always zero). \(\square \)

7 A family of \(\textbf{O}\)-functors for \(p=2\)

In this section, we continue assuming that \(\operatorname {char}(\Bbbk )=2\). Before going into full detail, let us state the principal outcome of this section in simple terms.

Theorem 7.0.1

Let \(\alpha \in \Bbbk \) be a root of the polynomial \(X^2+X+1\). There is a unique LSM functor \(\operatorname {Rep}C_2^2\rightarrow \operatorname {Ver}_4\) that does not send \(A_1([\alpha :1])\) to zero. Taking the transitive subgroup \(C_2^2<S_4\) then produces a \(\operatorname {Frob}^2\)-LSM functor

$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal {C}\xrightarrow {X\mapsto X^{\otimes 4}}\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Rep}C_2^2\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_4 \end{aligned}$$

that commutes with all tensor functors. The functor is exact for \(\mathcal {C}=\operatorname {Ver}_4\).

This is the realisation of Conjecture 5.4.2 for \(p=2=n\), and is proved in Theorem 6.1.2 and Proposition 7.2.1. It is a plausible candidate to detect fibering over \(\operatorname {Ver}_4\) by Theorem 7.3.3.

More generally, for each \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\backslash \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\), we use Theorem 5.2.1 to obtain an \(\textbf{O}^2_2\)-functor \(\Phi ^\lambda _1\) from the \(\textbf{V}\)-functor \(\Theta _1^\lambda \) in Corollary 6.1.3. For all other cases in Corollary 6.1.3 we similarly obtain an \(\textbf{O}^2\{\mathcal {V}\}\)-functor \(\Phi ^\lambda _m\) or \(\Phi _\infty \), for \(\mathcal {V}\) some tannakian category. By taking the descendant along the fibre functor, we thus have associated \(\textbf{O}^2_1\)-functors.

Lemma 7.0.2

Let \(\mathcal {C}\) be a tensor category and fix \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\) and \(m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\).

  1. (1)

    If \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(\Phi _\infty \)-exact, it is also \(\Phi _\infty ^\lambda \)-exact.

  2. (2)

    If \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(\Phi _\infty ^\lambda \)-exact, it is also \(\Phi _m^\lambda \)-exact.

  3. (3)

    If \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(\Phi _{m+1}^\lambda \)-exact, it is also \(\Phi _m^\lambda \)-exact.

Proof

This follows directly from Proposition 5.2.3(1) and Lemma 6.3.7. \(\square \)

In the rest of the section we obtain more refined results about these exactness criteria.

Remark 7.0.3

The functor \(\Phi _1^\lambda \) for \(\lambda \not \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\) is precisely the conjectural \(\textbf{O}_2^2\)-functor from Conjecture 5.4.2 in the one case where the conjecture is proved thus far.

7.1 New characterisations of tannakian categories

Lemma 7.1.1

If a tensor category is \(\Phi _\infty \)-exact, then it is Frobenius exact.

Proof

In order to find a contradiction, we consider a \(\Phi _\infty \)-exact tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\) that is not Frobenius exact. By adjunction and Theorem 2.2.1 a tensor category is \(\Phi _\infty \)-exact if and only if no monomorphism \(\alpha :\textbf{1}\rightarrow X\) is annihilated by \(\Phi _\infty \). Using the notion of coinvariants from e.g. [5], it follows, for instance using an exact faithful functor \(\mathcal {C}\rightarrow \textrm{Vec}\), that \(\Phi _\infty (\alpha )\not =0\) if and only if the composite

$$\begin{aligned} \textbf{1}\xrightarrow {\alpha ^{\otimes 4}} X^{\otimes 4}\twoheadrightarrow \textrm{H}_0(C_2^2, X^{\otimes 4}), \end{aligned}$$

is non-zero. Here, the right-hand term represents the coinvariants with respect to the restriction of the braid action to \(C_2^2<S_4\). Since \(\mathcal {C}\) is not Frobenius exact, we have a monomorphism \(\alpha :\textbf{1}\rightarrow X \) with \(\operatorname {Fr}(\alpha )=0\), so also \(\operatorname {Fr}(\alpha )^{\otimes 2}=\operatorname {Fr}(\alpha ^{\otimes 2})=0\). In other words, the composite

$$\begin{aligned} \textbf{1}\xrightarrow {\alpha ^{\otimes 4}}X^{\otimes 4}\twoheadrightarrow \textrm{H}_0(C_2, X^{\otimes 4}) \end{aligned}$$

is zero, where \(C_2<C_2^2<S_4\) is generated by (13)(24), a contradiction. \(\square \)

Proposition 7.1.2

Let \(\mathcal {C}\) be a tensor category with one of the following properties

  1. (1)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) has property (P);

  2. (2)

    The \(\Phi _\infty \)-type of \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(\textrm{Vec}\subset \textrm{Vec}_{\mathbb {Z}}\).

  3. (3)

    Every object in \(\mathcal {C}\) is algebraic.

If \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(\Phi ^\lambda _\infty \)-exact, for some \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\), then it is also Frobenius exact and \(\Phi _\infty \)-exact.

Proof

By Lemma 7.1.1 it is sufficient to show that \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(\Phi _\infty \)-exact.

Part (1) follows from Lemma 6.3.7 and Proposition 5.2.3.

Denote by \(\mathcal {F}il\mathcal {C}\) the category of \(\mathbb {Z}\)-filtered objects in \(\mathcal {C}\), which we can identify with the category of C-comodules in the category of finite-dimensional filtered vector spaces \(\mathcal {F}\), if \(\mathcal {C}\) is equivalent to the category of C-comodules for a coalgebra C. Hence Proposition 6.3.6 implies there exists an LSM functor \(\mathcal {C}\rightarrow \mathcal {F}il \mathcal {C}\) such that the solid arrows below yield a commutative diagram of LSM functors

(7.1)

The functor \(\mathcal {F}il\mathcal {C}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\boxtimes \textrm{Vec}_{\mathbb {Z}}\) is given by taking the associated \(\mathbb {Z}\)-graded object and the functor \(\mathcal {F}il\mathcal {C}\rightarrow \mathcal {C}\) is given by forgetting the filtration.

The above considerations give a second proof for part (1), as an object in \(\mathcal {F}il\mathcal {C}\) is annihilated by the functor to \(\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \textrm{Vec}\) if and only if it is annihilated by the functor to \(\mathcal {C}\), so we can apply Lemma 2.2.2.

Under assumption (2), all \(\mathbb {Z}\)-filtrations of objects in the image of \(\mathcal {C}\rightarrow \mathcal {F}il\mathcal {C}\) are trivial, and we can identify \(\Phi _\infty \) and \(\Phi ^\lambda _\infty \), either by forgetting the \(\mathbb {Z}\)-grading on \(\textrm{Vec}_{\mathbb {Z}}\) or embedding \(\textrm{Vec}\) into \(\textrm{Vec}_{\mathbb {Z}}\). This implies that \(\mathcal {C}\) is also \(\Phi _\infty \)-exact, concluding the proof of case (2).

Finally, we can observe that the assumption in (3) implies the assumption in (2), so we can reduce to the previous case. \(\square \)

Proposition 7.1.2 raises the following question.

Question 7.1.3

Is the \(\Phi _\infty \)-type of every tensor category (of moderate growth) \(\textrm{Vec}\subset \textrm{Vec}_{\mathbb {Z}}\)?

Proposition 7.1.4

For a tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\), a fixed \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\) and \(m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\), with \(m>1\) in case \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_4)\backslash \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\), consider the following 5 conditions:

  1. (a)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) is tannakian;

  2. (b)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) is Frobenius exact;

  3. (c)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(\Phi _\infty \)-exact;

  4. (d)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(\Phi _\infty ^\lambda \)-exact;

  5. (e)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(\Phi _m^\lambda \)-exact.

Then we have the following implications:

  1. (1)

    If \(\mathcal {C}\) is of moderate growth, then (a), (b) and (c) are equivalent.

  2. (2)

    If \(\mathcal {C}\) satisfies (P), then (c) and (d) are equivalent.

  3. (3)

    If \(\mathcal {C}\) is finite and the \(\operatorname {Ver}_{2^\infty }\)-conjecture is valid, then all (a) – (e) are equivalent.

Proof

Part (1) follows from Theorem 2.3.4, Lemma 7.1.1 and Remark 4.2.2(3).

Part (2) follows from Lemma 7.0.2(2) and Proposition 7.1.2(1).

For part (3), we can use parts (1) and (2), so it suffices to observe that (d) implies (e) by Lemma 7.0.2(1), and that (e) implies (a). The latter follows from Lemma 4.3.6 for \(n=1\), and the fact that \(\operatorname {Ver}_8^+\) is not \(\Phi ^\lambda _m\)-exact by Proposition 7.2.1 below. \(\square \)

7.2 Applications to incompressible categories

Following [1], we set

$$\mathcal {C}_{2i}=\operatorname {Ver}_{2^{i+1}},\quad \text{ and }\quad \mathcal {C}_{2i+1}=\operatorname {Ver}_{2^{i+2}}^+, \quad \text { for }i\in \mathbb {N}, $$

yielding a chain \(\mathcal {C}_{j}\subset \mathcal {C}_{j+1}\) of incompressible tensor categories.

Proposition 7.2.1

Consider \(j\in \mathbb {N}\), \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\) and \(m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\), then \(\mathcal {C}_j\) is \(\Phi _m^\lambda \)-exact if and only if

  1. (1)

    \(j=0\) (i.e. \(\mathcal {C}_j=\textrm{Vec}\)), or

  2. (2)

    \(j\le 2\) (i.e. \(\mathcal {C}_j\subset \operatorname {Ver}_4\)) and \(m=1\) and \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_4)\backslash \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\).

The crucial input for the proof is the following direct computation. Denote by V the projective simple object in \(\operatorname {Ver}_4\) and P the projective cover of \(\textbf{1}\).

Lemma 7.2.2

Let \(\alpha \) be a generator of \(\mathbb {F}_4\), viewed as an element in \(\Bbbk \subset \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\). As \(C_2^2<S_4\)-representations, we have

$$\begin{aligned} \operatorname {Hom}_{\operatorname {Ver}_4}(P,V^{\otimes 4})\;\simeq \; A_1(\alpha )\oplus A_1(\alpha +1). \end{aligned}$$

Proof of Proposition 7.2.1

By the chain of inclusions, for any given \((m,\lambda )\) there is an \(l\in \mathbb {N}\) such that \(\mathcal {C}_j\) is exact if and only if \(j\le l\). As the simple projective object in \(\mathcal {C}_2\) tensor squares to the projective cover of \(\textbf{1}\) in \(\mathcal {C}_1\) it also follows from Lemma 2.2.2 that \(\mathcal {C}_1\) is \(\Phi _m^\lambda \)-exact if and only if \(\mathcal {C}_2\) is \(\Phi _m^\lambda \)-exact.

By Lemma 7.2.2 and Proposition 5.2.4 it follows that \(\mathcal {C}_2=\operatorname {Ver}_4\) is \(\Phi _m^\lambda \)-exact if and only if \(m=1\) and \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_4)\backslash \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\).

By the combination of the previous two paragraphs it is now sufficient to prove that \(\mathcal {C}_3\) is not \(\Phi _1^\lambda \)-exact for \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_4)\backslash \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\). This follows from Lemma 4.3.5 and the observation that \(\Phi _1^\lambda \) satisfies (O1) for \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_4)\backslash \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\), as follows from Lemma 7.2.2 and Corollary 2.3.7. \(\square \)
