Corollary 7.2.3

Consider projective objects P, Q in \(\mathcal {C}_i\) for \(i>2\), then the \(C_2^2\)-representation \(\operatorname {Hom}_{\mathcal {C}_i}(P,Q^{\otimes 4})\) is a direct sum of non-trivial permutation modules, i.e. a direct sum of modules isomorphic to \(A_1(0)\), \(A_1(1)\), \(A_1(\infty )\), or \(\Bbbk C_2^2\).

Proof

By Proposition 7.2.1 and Proposition 5.2.4, we have

$$\begin{aligned} \Theta ^\lambda _m(\operatorname {Hom}_{\mathcal {C}_i}(P,Q^{\otimes 4}))=0 \end{aligned}$$

for all \(m>0\) and \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\). The conclusion then follows from the definition of \(\Theta ^\lambda _m\) and the classification of indecomposable modules. \(\square \)

Proposition 7.2.4

Fix \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\backslash \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\).

  1. (1)

    \(\overline{\Phi ^\lambda _1}\) is the descendant of \(\Phi _2^\lambda \) obtained from the fibre functor \(\operatorname {Rep}\alpha _2\rightarrow \textrm{Vec}\).

  2. (2)

    \(\Phi ^\lambda _1\) satisfies (O1) if and only if \(\lambda \in \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_4)\).

Proof

Part (1) follows from the classification in Theorem 6.1.2 and the observation that \(\Theta _1^\lambda (A_3(\lambda ))\simeq \textbf{1}^2\), so \(\Theta _1^\lambda (A_3(\lambda ))\) is not negligible. The latter observation can be computed directly, but also follows from Lemma 6.2.4, which shows that symmetric monoidal functors from the additive monoidal subcategory generated by \(A_3(\lambda )\) in \(\operatorname {Stab}C_2^2\) take values in tannakian subcategories, so \(\Theta _1^\lambda (A_3(\lambda ))\in \textrm{Vec}\subset \operatorname {Ver}_4\).

Part (2) was already observed in (the proof of) Proposition 7.2.1. \(\square \)

7.3 Conjectural characterisation of categories that fibre over \(\operatorname {Ver}_4\)

For this section we fix a generator \(\alpha \in \mathbb {F}_4\), which we interpret as an element of \(\Bbbk \subset \mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\), or more precisely of \(\mathbb {P}^1(\Bbbk )\backslash \mathbb {P}^1(\mathbb {F}_2)\).

Conjecture 7.3.1

The following conditions are equivalent on a tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\):

  1. (1)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(\Phi ^\alpha _1\)-exact and of moderate growth;

  2. (2)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) admits a tensor functor to \(\operatorname {Ver}_4\).

Note that (2) implies (1) in Conjecture 7.3.1, by Proposition 7.2.1. We discuss some relations with other conjectures and statements:

Theorem 7.3.2

The following statements are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    Conjecture 7.3.1 is true;

  2. (2)

    \(\Phi _1^\alpha \) satisfies (O2);

  3. (3)

    A tensor category of moderate growth is tannakian if and only if it is \(\Phi _2^\alpha \)-exact.

Proof

That (1) implies (2) follows from Proposition 7.2.4(2) and Theorem 4.3.2(2). That (2) implies (1) follows from Proposition 7.2.4(2) and Theorem 4.3.3.

That (2) and (3) are equivalent follows from Proposition 7.2.4(1). \(\square \)

Finally, we show that Conjecture 7.3.1, specialised to finite tensor categories, is a consequence of [2, Conjecture 1.4].

Theorem 7.3.3

Assume the \(\operatorname {Ver}_{2^\infty }\)-Conjecture is valid. The following conditions are equivalent on a finite tensor category \(\mathcal {C}\):

  1. (1)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(\Phi _1^\alpha \)-exact;

  2. (2)

    \(\mathcal {C}\) admits a tensor functor to \(\operatorname {Ver}_4\);

  3. (3)

    There exist projective objects \(P,Q\in \mathcal {C}\) so that the \(C_2^2\)-representation \(\operatorname {Hom}(Q,P^{\otimes 4})\) has an indecomposable summand in the list

    $$\begin{aligned} \{\Omega ^{i}\textbf{1}\mid i\in \mathbb {Z}\}\,\cup \, \{A_m(\alpha )\mid m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\}\,\cup \, \{A_m(1+\alpha )\mid m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\}; \end{aligned}$$
  4. (4)

    There exist projective objects \(P,Q\in \mathcal {C}\) so that the \(C_2^2\)-representation \(\operatorname {Hom}(Q,P^{\otimes 4})\) has an indecomposable summand in the list

    $$\begin{aligned} \{\textbf{1}, A_1(\alpha ), A_2(\alpha )\}. \end{aligned}$$

Proof

By Proposition 7.2.4(2), equivalence of (1) and (2) is a special case of Proposition 4.3.4. In particular this means that \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(\Phi ^\alpha _1\)-exact if and only if it is \(\Phi ^{\alpha +1}_1\)-exact.

Clearly (4) implies (3). To prove that (3) implies (1), by the previous paragraph it suffices to show that under assumption (3) \(\mathcal {C}\) is either \(\Phi ^{\alpha }_1\)-exact or \(\Phi ^{\alpha +1}_1\)-exact. If one of the modules \(\Omega ^i\textbf{1}\) or \(A_m(\alpha )\) appears in \(\operatorname {Hom}(Q,P^{\otimes 4})\), then \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(\Phi _1^\alpha \)-exact by Proposition 5.2.4. If \(A_m(1+\alpha )\) appears, \(\mathcal {C}\) must likewise be \(\Phi ^{\alpha +1}_1\)-exact.

Now we prove that (2) implies (4). Assume first that \(\mathcal {C}\) is tannakian, then writing the forgetful tensor functor \(\mathcal {C}\rightarrow \textrm{Vec}\) as \(\operatorname {Hom}_{\mathcal {C}}(P,-)\) for some projective object P, shows that \(\textbf{1}\) appears as a \(C_2^2\)-summand in \(\operatorname {Hom}_{\mathcal {C}}(P,Q^{\otimes 4})\), for any projective object \(Q\in \mathcal {C}\).

Now assume that \(\mathcal {C}\) is not tannakian, but has a tensor functor to \(\operatorname {Ver}_4\). In particular, \(\Phi _1^\alpha \) is faithful on \(\mathcal {C}\). Hence, by Proposition 5.2.4, there must be P, Q as in (3) so that \(\Omega ^i\textbf{1}\) or \(A_m(\alpha )\), for some \(i\in \mathbb {Z}\) or \(m\in \mathbb {Z}_{>0}\), appears in \(\operatorname {Hom}_\mathcal {C}(P,Q^{\otimes 4})\). However, if \(\Omega ^i\textbf{1}\) or \(A_{m+1}(\alpha )\) for \(m>1\) appeared, it would follow, again from Proposition 5.2.4, that \(\mathcal {C}\) is \(\Phi _m^\alpha \)-exact and hence tannakian by Proposition 7.1.4(3), contradicting our assumption. Hence only \(A_1(\alpha )\) and \(A_2(\alpha )\) are allowed to appear in this case. \(\square \)

Remark 7.3.4

If we assume the \(\operatorname {Ver}_{2^\infty }\)-conjecture to be true, there is an alternative (conjectural) characterisation of tensor categories that fibre over \(\operatorname {Ver}_4\), namely as those that have Frobenius order at most 1, see [17, §10]. At the moment, it is not clear whether it is unconditionally true that \(\Phi _1^\alpha \)-exactness implies that the Frobenius order is at most 1, or the other way around.

Notes

  1. We use the letter \(\textbf{O}\), and subsequently \(\textbf{V}\) in the next section, as a reference to Victor Ostrik, who in [22] was the first to introduce, and demonstrate the central role of, the first example of an \(\textbf{O}^i\{\mathcal {V}\}\)-functor, the Frobenius functor.

  2. To do this rigorously, one needs to interpret the occurrence of \(\Phi _{\mathcal {C}}\) that acts as ‘F’ as a \(\Bbbk \)-linear tensor functor \(\mathcal {C}\rightarrow (\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n})'\), where \((\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n})'\) is the same additive monoidal category as \(\mathcal {C}\boxtimes \operatorname {Ver}_{p^n}\) but with \(\Bbbk \)-linear structure twisted via the appropriate power of the Frobenius automorphism.
